case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was ultimately found to have HIV infection (CD4 = 38) – a disease on the SELECTED list (hiv_aids). Although disseminated coccidioidomycosis is the primary cause of death, it is not on the SELECTED list, so the target diagnosis for this teaching case is HIV/AIDS.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the case presentation just before the HIV laboratory results are disclosed (“Further testing showed that he was positive for HIV‑1…”). All preceding data (clinical picture, imaging, initial labs, and the infectious‑disease physician’s suspicion of coccidioidomycosis) give enough clues (severe miliary infection, profound weight loss, lymphadenopathy, shock) to prompt consideration of underlying HIV‑associated immunosuppression, without revealing the diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically ruled out lymphoma, tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, and cryptococcosis with imaging, cultures, antigen testing, and special stains; they pursued coccidioidomycosis serology based on endemic exposure; the HIV diagnosis explained the disseminated fungal pattern and guided the final autopsy confirmation.
case_prompt:
Our patient was a 61‑year‑old Hispanic man who had not seen a health‑care provider in many years and presented with a one‑month history of vague abdominal pain, 20‑lb weight loss, generalized weakness with malaise, occasional cough that became productive of clear sputum over the last week, occasional nausea and non‑bloody diarrhea, and arthralgias. He denied fevers, chills, or rash. He was born in Chihuahua, Mexico, and had lived in Texas since age seven. He worked for five years in a ceramic and tile factory with high‑intensity dust exposure without respiratory protection. He was evaluated a few days earlier by a private physician who prescribed ciprofloxacin and metronidazole without diagnostic testing, with no improvement, prompting presentation to the emergency department.

In the emergency department his temperature was 98.3 °F, blood pressure 84/61 mmHg, pulse 128/min, respiratory rate 27/min, and pulse oximetry 92 % on room air. He appeared acutely ill but was alert. Lung examination was limited by COVID‑19 restrictions; there were decreased breath sounds without rales. Cervical, supraclavicular, inguinal, and axillary lymph nodes were markedly enlarged, some >3 cm. Laboratory studies showed: WBC 8,900/mm³ (80 % neutrophils, 0.5 % bands, 11 % eosinophils), hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, hematocrit 27.6 %, platelets 447 × 10³/mm³; metabolic panel with bicarbonate 17 mmol/L, BUN 54 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, albumin 2.2 g/dL; lipase 14 U/L, lactate 2.5 mmol/L, ALT 57 U/L, AST 139 U/L; procalcitonin 6.1 ng/mL.

Chest radiograph revealed a diffuse micronodular pattern, prompting a COVID‑19 test that was negative. Non‑contrast chest CT demonstrated extensive diffuse bilateral micronodules in a miliary pattern, mediastinal and axillary lymphadenopathy with pericardial thickening. Abdomen and pelvis CT showed enlarged para‑aortic, gastrohepatic, inguinal, external and internal iliac lymph nodes. The patient was evaluated for lymphoma and tuberculosis while receiving empiric vancomycin, cefepime, IV fluids, and methylprednisolone. Blood and urine cultures were obtained. The infectious‑disease physician suspected coccidioidomycosis and initiated serologic testing. Histoplasma antigen, acid‑fast bacilli smear, and cryptococcal antibody tests were ordered and later returned negative. Sputum culture grew Candida albicans. Despite aggressive supportive care, the patient required vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Disseminated fungal infection (coccidioidomycosis) was suspected because of endemic exposure and miliary lung nodules; the team “began a work up for the patient with serologic testing” for coccidioidomycosis. |
2. Tuberculosis remained a chief concern given the miliary pattern; the authors note the patient was “seen by many physicians to rule out lymphoma and tuberculosis.” |
3. Lymphoma was considered due to extensive peripheral lymphadenopathy; however, initial imaging and lack of malignant cells on cultures did not support it. |
4. Histoplasmosis was evaluated with antigen testing, which “did not yield a positive result.” |
5. Cryptococcosis was considered in the differential for AIDS‑related opportunistic infection, but “Cryptococcus antibody tests did not yield a positive result.” |
6. COVID‑19 was initially entertained because of the diffuse micronodular chest film, but “COVID‑19… turned out to be negative.” |
7. Bacterial sepsis was addressed empirically with vancomycin and cefepime, but cultures were unrevealing, and the high procalcitonin was attributed to severe infection rather than a specific bacterial pathogen. |
8. Underlying HIV infection explained the disseminated opportunistic infection pattern; later testing confirmed HIV‑1 with high viral load and CD4 = 38, indicating AIDS. |

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has confirmed latent tuberculosis infection (positive TST and IGRA) with sufficient laboratory evidence; tuberculosis is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore, the primary target diagnosis is tuberculosis (LTBI) (selected disease). IgG4‑related disease is the accompanying OUT_OF_SCOPE condition.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include the full clinical history, imaging findings, laboratory results (including IgG, IgG4, autoantibodies, CSF, TST, IGRA, sputum, chest CT) up to the point where the authors present the positive TB screening results but stop before the sentence that states the definitive diagnosis (“We diagnosed the patient with IgG4‑RD complicated with LTBI”) and before treatment details. This provides all data needed to infer latent TB infection without revealing the diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: • Initial imaging suggested meningioma (dural tail sign) → histopathology and IgG4 immunostaining redirected diagnosis to IgG4‑RD. • Prior tubercular meningitis treatment failed → lack of CSF mycobacteria and absence of caseating granulomas argued against active TB. • Positive TST/IGRA with negative sputum, chest CT, and no systemic TB signs distinguished latent infection from active disease. • Broad autoimmune serology panel was negative, ruling out other systemic vasculitides or connective‑tissue diseases.
case_prompt: A 40‑year‑old man presented with intermittent headache and diplopia. Six years earlier he had recurrent frontal and top‑of‑head headaches and was diagnosed with tubercular meningitis at a local hospital, receiving a 2‑month HRZE regimen followed by 27 months of HRE. His headache persisted, and three years ago he sought care at our institution. Contrast‑enhanced MRI showed an enhancing clival mass with a dural tail sign, initially thought to be a meningioma; he underwent gamma‑knife surgery, which only partially relieved his headache. Seven months before his current presentation he developed progressively worsening diplopia, hoarseness, and dysphagia. Examination revealed bitemporal hemianopsia and limited bilateral eye abduction, without speech disturbance or motor deficits. Repeat contrast‑enhancing MRI demonstrated a 3.8 × 2.9 × 2.9 cm clival mass with dural tail, compressing the brainstem, eroding the clivus and left occipital condyle, and extending into the nasopharynx. Cerebrospinal fluid was essentially normal; mycobacterial and cryptococcal organisms were not detected. Endoscopic subtotal resection was performed. Histopathology showed fibro‑connective tissue with mixed inflammation dominated by plasma cells; immunostaining revealed >200 IgG4‑positive plasma cells per high‑power field and an IgG4‑to‑CD138 ratio of ~55 %. No caseating granulomas were seen. Serum studies showed IgG 17.2 g/L (reference 8.0‑15.5) and IgG4 1.9 g/L (reference 0.035‑1.5). ANA was 1:100; anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti‑SSA, anti‑SSB, anti‑dsDNA, anti‑Smith, anti‑Scl‑70 and other ENA antibodies were negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen, HBV DNA, and HCV antibody were negative. Tuberculin skin test was positive (induration ≥ 10 mm) and TB‑IGRA yielded an IFN‑γ level of 414.21 pg/mL (reference 0‑14). Repeated sputum examinations were negative. Chest CT showed no pulmonary lesions or mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy. Evaluation for other systemic manifestations of IgG4‑related disease was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Meningioma considered because the mass had a dural tail sign on MRI, “initially considered to be a meningioma based on its imaging appearance.” Histopathology lacked typical meningioma features and instead showed abundant IgG4‑positive plasma cells, ruling it out. |
2. Active tubercular meningitis revisited due to prior diagnosis, but CSF was normal, “mycobacterium spp. … were not detected,” and no caseating granulomas were found, making active CNS TB unlikely. |
3. Active pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis evaluated because of TB exposure, yet chest CT was negative for lesions, sputum cultures repeatedly negative, and “no granuloma with caseous necrosis was noted,” arguing against active disease. |
4. Cryptococcal infection screened given CNS involvement; CSF cryptococcal test was negative, excluding this pathogen. |
5. Systemic autoimmune vasculitides and connective‑tissue diseases considered; negative serologies (“anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti‑SS‑A, … all negative”) excluded these differentials. |
6. Latent tuberculosis infection supported by a positive tuberculin skin test and markedly elevated IGRA (“TST was positive… TB‑IGRA demonstrated significantly elevated IFN‑γ (414.21 pg/mL)”), in the absence of active disease signs, confirming LTBI as the appropriate TB diagnosis.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately had disseminated Mycobacterium bovis BCG infection, which falls under the selected disease “tuberculosis.” No out‑of‑scope disease is required as the primary mystery.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the lung‑biopsy pathology results are disclosed. Include the chief complaint, progressive constitutional symptoms, physical findings, imaging, BAL results, laboratory abnormalities, empiric antimicrobial therapy, and the decision to obtain a lung biopsy, but omit the paragraph that states the biopsy revealed M. bovis BCG (and Cryptococcus).
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished TB/BCG infection from Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, bacterial sepsis, viral infection, Cryptococcus infection, HIV infection, chronic granulomatous disease, and inherited IFN‑γ pathway defects by using microbiologic cultures/PCR, histopathology, serology, functional assays, and extensive genetic testing.
case_prompt: A 48‑year‑old Caucasian man with a history of grade 1‑2 follicular lymphoma treated with R‑CHOP and Rituximab presented with progressive asthenia, anorexia and a 12‑kg weight loss over nine months. Seven months after his last Rituximab infusion he developed fever, splenomegaly (17 cm) and fine dry crackles with dyspnea (NYHA class II‑IV). Chest CT showed an interstitial lung disease with nodular lesions and pulmonary function tests demonstrated a decline in alveolar gas exchange. Broncho‑alveolar lavage yielded an alveolar lymphocytosis (230 000 cells/mL, 67 % lymphocytes, 28 % macrophages) with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio; PCR testing was negative for viruses and cultures were negative for bacteria and parasites. Laboratory studies revealed an inflammatory syndrome, acute renal failure, pancytopenia with severe lymphopenia, mild neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia and hypogammaglobulinemia. Bone‑marrow aspiration showed poor cellularity without malignant cells. Empiric therapy with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (positive Pneumocystis jirovecii PCR in BAL) and piperacillin‑tazobactam was started, and corticosteroids were added, leading to transient respiratory improvement. Despite this, the patient’s condition worsened with progressive hypoxemia, prompting a lung biopsy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered due to positive PCR in BAL; treated with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim. | “sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim for Pneumocysis jirovecii PCR+ in BAL”.
2. Bacterial pneumonia considered; broad‑spectrum piperacillin/tazobactam administered empirically. | “large-spectrum antibacterial therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam”.
3. Viral infection considered but excluded by negative PCR screening of BAL fluid. | “without any virus (screened by PCR)”.
4. HIV infection ruled out as a predisposing factor; serology and PCR were negative. | “HIV PCR and serology were negative”.
5. Chronic granulomatous disease evaluated; normal phagocytosis assays excluded it. | “Phagocytosis assays were normal, discarding the hypothesis of chronic granulomatous disease”.
6. Cryptococcosis identified later in lung tissue but lacked CNS involvement, making it a secondary finding rather than the primary cause of the severe presentation. | “Cryptococcus neoformans was also identified in lung biopsy but without central nervous system involvement”.
7. Primary/secondary IFN‑γ pathway defect hypothesized; extensive functional assays and whole‑exome sequencing showed no anti‑IFN‑γ autoantibodies, normal STAT1 phosphorylation, and no pathogenic mutations, thus not supporting this as the sole cause. | “These results suggested for the absence of anti‑IFNgamma autoantibodies… STAT1 phosphorylation … was preserved… Whole exome sequencing … did not reveal … mutations … involved in MSMD”.
8. Disseminated Mycobacterium bovis BCG infection ultimately identified in lung tissue (Ziehl‑Neelsen stain, PCR, culture) and also recovered from bone‑marrow and blood cultures, providing a unifying diagnosis for the systemic illness. | “A lung biopsy was performed that finally revealed invasive infection by M. bovis BCG, suspected by Ziehl‑Neelsen coloration and confirmed by PCR and culture… The M. bovis BCG strain was also found in the bone marrow and blood cultures”.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has several diseases on the SELECTED list (HIV infection, COVID‑19, cryptococcosis, tuberculosis). The primary diagnostic challenge presented in the report—requiring synthesis of clinical, radiographic, and laboratory data before definitive microbiology—is the identification of disseminated **tuberculosis**. Therefore, the target diagnosis is tuberculosis (selected disease).
2. Breakpoint: Include presentation, vital signs, physical examination, and all initial investigations up to the point where sputum was obtained for GeneXpert and cultures, but omit the GeneXpert result and any later therapeutic details. This provides sufficient information (miliary pattern on CXR, positive urine LAM, HIV with CD4 32) for the learner to deduce tuberculosis without revealing the definitive test outcome.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors confirmed tuberculosis using urine LAM positivity, characteristic miliary infiltrates on chest radiography, and a later positive GeneXpert. They distinguished it from COVID‑19 pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, and Pneumocystis pneumonia by integrating imaging patterns, specific antigen tests, and the patient’s immunologic status.
case_prompt:
A 37‑year‑old nulliparous woman with a recent diagnosis of HIV infection (not on antiretroviral therapy) presented to Mulago National Referral Hospital COVID‑19 Treatment Unit with a three‑day history of worsening cough and dyspnea. She reported a productive, mucoid cough, evening fevers, and a two‑month history of weight loss. The referral note also recorded anosmia, high‑grade intermittent fevers, headaches, altered mentation, a loss of consciousness episode, and myalgias for five days. Four days before admission a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR and rapid antigen test; she had tested HIV‑positive eight days prior and was not receiving cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.

On admission she was critically ill: axillary temperature 38.5 °C, pulse 168 bpm, respiratory rate 32 /min, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, oxygen saturation 85‑90 % on 5 L /min nasal prongs. She was febrile, tachypneic, with nasal flaring and intercostal recessions. Bilateral coarse crepitations were auscultated. Neurologically she was restless, Glasgow coma scale 8/15 (E3 V2 M3), with neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign. Other systems were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed: white blood cell count 11.8 × 10³/µL (neutrophils 91.6 %, lymphocytes 4.5 %), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL (MCV 67 fL), platelets 300 × 10³/µL, normal renal and liver panels, blood group B Rh D positive. CD4⁺ count was 32 cells/µL. Serum and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen tests were positive. Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) test was positive (Grade II). Chest radiography demonstrated miliary nodular infiltrates with superimposed ground‑glass opacities. Non‑contrast brain CT revealed a large right frontoparietotemporal hypodense area consistent with a right middle cerebral artery territory infarct. Sputum and blood samples were obtained for GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing and cultures (results pending).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 pneumonia considered because of recent positive SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR, but the chest radiograph showed a miliary pattern rather than the typical bilateral peripheral ground‑glass opacities of COVID‑19 pneumonia. | "Chest radiography revealed features of miliary tuberculosis with background ground glass opacities."
2. Bacterial community‑acquired pneumonia was contemplated given fever, productive cough, and neutrophilia, yet the diffuse millet‑seed nodules on imaging and lack of lobar consolidation made this less likely. | "Chest radiography revealed features of miliary tuberculosis..."
3. Cryptococcal meningitis supported by positive CSF cryptococcal antigen and meningeal signs, explaining the altered mental status, but it does not account for the respiratory findings and miliary pattern. | "Her serum and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) tests were positive."
4. Disseminated tuberculosis – favored owing to (a) positive urine LAM in an advanced‑HIV patient, (b) classic miliary infiltrates on chest X‑ray, (c) high‑risk immunosuppression (CD4 32), and (d) pending GeneXpert sample from sputum. | "The urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) was positive (Grade II)... Chest radiography revealed features of miliary tuberculosis..."
5. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered in HIV with low CD4, but typical radiographic findings are diffuse bilateral ground‑glass without miliary nodules, and urine LAM positivity steered diagnosis away. | "Chest radiography revealed features of miliary tuberculosis with background ground glass opacities."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on a post‑infectious sixth nerve palsy attributed to recent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection. COVID‑19 is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is covid_19.  
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation, history of recent respiratory illness, family members with confirmed COVID‑19, neurologic exam, MRI findings, routine CSF analysis, extensive multiplex PCR panels (negative for other pathogens), negative SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR from oropharyngeal swab, and the positive SARS‑CoV‑2 IgG in serum and CSF. Stop before the authors’ concluding sentence that explicitly states “post‑infectious abducens nerve palsy appeared to be the most likely diagnosis.”  
3. Key analytic distinctions: The authors used (a) negative inflammatory markers and MRI without signs of intracranial inflammation or raised pressure to rule out inflammatory or mass lesions; (b) broad multiplex PCR panels and serology to exclude bacterial, fungal, tick‑borne, and other viral pathogens; (c) negative SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR with positive serum/CSF IgG and a negative intrathecal antibody index to argue for a systemic, post‑infectious mechanism rather than direct viral neuro‑invasion; (d) clinical context of close exposure to a PCR‑confirmed case and prior respiratory symptoms to support recent COVID‑19 infection.
case_prompt:
In January 2021, a 2‑year‑old boy of white Caucasian origin presented to his local ophthalmologist for acute unilateral sixth‑nerve palsy and was transferred to the pediatric emergency department. He had a sudden left‑eye lateral movement dysfunction with continuous abduction deficit and a fixated head turn to the left. He was otherwise fit, with no trauma, headache, vomiting, fever, or chronic disease, and his vaccination status was complete. Three weeks earlier he experienced a respiratory tract infection lasting two weeks with increased respiratory rate, dry cough, intermittent fever, and loss of appetite, managed symptomatically as a common cold. During that period his father and uncle developed cough, dyspnea, sore throat, and muscle aches; the uncle tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by PCR after close indoor contact with the child 4 days before his positive test. The relatives were unvaccinated.

On admission, C‑reactive protein was negative; full blood count showed mild thrombocytopenia (186 × 10⁹/L) but was otherwise normal. Contrast‑enhanced cranial MRI demonstrated a hypoplastic left abducens nerve and atrophy of the left lateral rectus muscle, without signs of inflammatory intracranial process, elevated intracranial pressure, or papilledema. Lumbar puncture revealed opening pressure of 24 cm H₂O; CSF routine studies were normal and oligoclonal bands absent. Multiplex‑PCR of CSF was negative for CMV, enterovirus, HSV‑1/2, HHV‑6, parechovirus, VZV, Cryptococcus spp., E. coli K1, H. influenzae, L. monocytogenes, N. meningitidis, S. agalactiae, and S. pneumoniae. Oropharyngeal swab multiplex‑PCR was negative for adenovirus, coronaviruses 229E/HKU1/NL63/OC43, human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus/enterovirus, influenza A/B, MERS‑CoV, SARS‑CoV‑2, parainfluenza 1‑4, RSV, Bordetella pertussis/parapertussis, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Borrelia burgdorferi serology was negative in serum and CSF. EEG was unremarkable. Ophthalmologic exams confirmed left sixth‑nerve palsy with incomitant squint angles; retraction syndrome was deemed unlikely because of sudden onset and absent globe retraction. Real‑time RT‑PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 from an oropharyngeal swab was negative, but serology was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 anti‑spike IgG, and SARS‑CoV‑2‑specific IgG was also detected in CSF. Pathogen‑specific antibody index was negative, and SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR from CSF was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Trauma‑related sixth‑nerve palsy unlikely | "His medical history was unremarkable for trauma, headache, vomiting or fever."
2. Intracranial mass or inflammatory lesion unlikely | "MRI showed ... no signs suggesting any inflammatory intracranial process or elevated intracranial pressure, no papilledema."
3. Bacterial meningitis/meningoencephalitis excluded | "Multiplex‑PCR from CSF was negative for ... E. coli K1, H. influenzae, L. monocytogenes, N. meningitidis, S. agalactiae, and S. pneumoniae."
4. Viral encephalitis (CMV, HSV, HHV‑6, VZV, enterovirus, parechovirus) excluded | "Multiplex‑PCR from CSF was negative for cytomegalovirus, enterovirus, herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, human herpesvirus 6, human parechovirus, varicella zoster virus..."
5. Fungal infection (Cryptococcus) excluded | "...Cryptococcus neoformans and gattii..."
6. Tick‑borne Lyme disease excluded | "Testing for Borrelia burgdorferi showed no antibodies in neither serum nor CSF."
7. Other respiratory viruses excluded | "Multiplex‑PCR performed on an oropharyngeal swab sample yielded a negative result for adenovirus, coronaviruses 229E, HKU1, NL63 and OC43, human metapneumovirus, human rhino‑/enterovirus, influenza virus A and B, MERS‑CoV, SARS‑CoV‑2..."
8. Direct SARS‑CoV‑2 CNS infection unlikely | "rRT‑PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 from CSF was negative" and "Pathogen‑specific antibody index ... was negative, suggesting involvement of central nervous system being secondary to systemic infection rather than direct viral infection."
9. Retraction syndrome unlikely | "An underlying retraction syndrome was considered unlikely due to the sudden onset of symptoms and absent globe retraction."
10. Post‑infectious COVID‑19 neuropathy most plausible | "Given the boy's history of recent respiratory tract infection, COVID‑19 very likely in his father and proven in his uncle, and detection of SARS‑CoV‑2‑IgG antibodies in the patient's serum and CSF..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), which falls under the selected disease “aspergillosis”. Hence the target diagnosis is aspergillosis (selected).
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all information up to the repeat chest CT showing an air‑crescent sign and the negative microbiologic work‑up, but stop before the authors explicitly state that “a diagnosis of IPA was highly likely.”
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: Diagnosis of IPA was supported by (a) imaging characteristic of multiple nodules with an air‑crescent sign, (b) clinical context of immunosuppression (high‑dose steroids, acute liver failure), (c) exclusion of bacterial, viral, and other fungal pathogens by negative cultures, serologies, BAL fluid studies and NGS, and (d) clinical response to antifungal therapy (caspofungin then voriconazole). Competing diagnoses were ruled out by the same negative microbiologic tests and lack of alternative radiologic patterns.
case_prompt:
A 17‑year‑old girl was admitted on 6 July 2020 with dysphoria, fatigue, vomiting, and jaundice that began 9 days earlier. She had been taking QubaiBabuqi tablets for vitiligo for more than 3 months before symptom onset. Physical examination showed severe jaundice of the skin and sclera and whitish facial patches; cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies on 7 July revealed total bilirubin 439.6 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 325.7 µmol/L, ALT 1174 U/L, AST 505 U/L, γ‑GT 131 U/L, ALP 166 U/L, PT 44.5 s, PTA 16 %, INR 4.84, and ammonia 258 µmol/L. A diagnosis of drug‑induced acute liver failure was made. On day 4 she developed hepatic encephalopathy and frequent vomiting, was placed on the liver‑transplant waiting list, and received dexamethasone, liver‑protective agents, and NBAL. Her liver function improved, and after 10 days in a comatose state she regained consciousness.

On 24 July she had intermittent low‑grade fever without cough. Laboratory tests showed total bilirubin 388 µmol/L, WBC 12.13 × 10⁹/L with 83.5 % neutrophils. A chest CT on 26 July demonstrated multiple nodules in both lungs. A repeat chest CT later showed an increase in the number of lung lesions and the appearance of an air‑crescent sign. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, a β‑D‑glucan (G) test, a galactomannan (GM) test, and next‑generation sequencing of respiratory samples were all negative. Blood cultures performed several times were negative. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, E, HIV, CMV, EBV, and HSV were negative, as were tests for autoimmune antibodies and other fungal antigens.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (target) is supported by characteristic CT findings of multiple nodules and an air‑crescent sign in an immunocompromised host. | "Chest CT scan showed multiple nodules in both lungs ... a repeat chest CT showed ... the presence of an air crescent sign."
2. Bacterial pneumonia was considered due to fever and neutrophilia, but repeatedly negative blood cultures made it unlikely. | "blood cultures ... were performed several times, and all tests were negative."
3. Other invasive fungal infections (e.g., mucormycosis, cryptococcosis) were excluded because BALF, G test, GM test, and NGS were all negative. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), G test, GM test, and next‑generation sequencing (NGS) were all negative."
4. Viral infections (CMV, EBV, HSV, hepatitis viruses, HIV) were ruled out by negative serologic and nucleic‑acid testing. | "Serological studies for hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), hepatitis E virus (HEV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative. Laboratory studies for cytomegalovirus nucleic acid (CMV‑DNA), Epstein‑Barr virus nucleic acid (EBV‑DNA), and herpes simplex virus (HSV) IgM antibody were negative."
5. Drug‑induced lung injury was not favored because imaging showed typical fungal patterns rather than diffuse infiltrates, and antifungal therapy led to radiologic improvement. | (implicit from case; no direct quote stating drug‑induced lung injury was considered, but the authors emphasized response to antifungal agents.)

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s central diagnostic challenge after the breakpoint is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. HIV infection is on the list but is presented only as a pre‑existing diagnosis without a new diagnostic work‑up; therefore, per Rule 4.1 the target diagnosis is the OUT_OF_SCOPE condition IRIS.  
2. Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the sentence “Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with IRIS.” Include the second admission’s clinical picture, vital signs, CSF data, and brain MRI findings that allow the reader to infer an inflammatory process despite microbial negativity.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished IRIS from recurrent cryptococcal meningitis or new opportunistic infection by (a) negative India‑ink stain and cultures, (b) modest CSF pleocytosis with low glucose ratio, (c) recent immune recovery (↑CD4, undetectable HIV load), and (d) meningeal enhancement on MRI that improved with lenalidomide.
case_prompt:
In June 2018, a 39‑year‑old man was admitted one day after being diagnosed with HIV infection because of two weeks of dizziness and vomiting. Physical exam showed temperature 37.5 °C, blood pressure 119/92 mmHg, pulse 112 bpm, respirations 20/min, stiff neck with positive meningeal signs. CD4 count was 7 cells/µL and HIV RNA 131,000 copies/mL. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure exceeded 400 mmH₂O; WBC 3 cells/µL, glucose 2.3 mmol/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, protein 0.426 g/L; CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.41. India‑ink staining and culture identified *Cryptococcus neoformans*, leading to a diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis (CM). A ventriculoperitoneal shunt relieved his symptoms. He received 2 weeks of amphotericin B 0.7 mg/kg/day plus flucytosine 100 mg/kg/day, followed by 8 weeks of fluconazole 400 mg/day; CSF cultures were negative after 10 days. HAART (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) began on hospital day 28 and he was discharged.

Follow‑up through March 2019 showed clinical stability, intracranial pressure 115–200 mmH₂O, CSF protein 1.06–2.53 g/L, WBC 5–10 cells/µL, glucose 2.0–2.8 mmol/L, CD4 82 cells/µL, and HIV RNA undetectable.

In April 2019 he developed headache and dizziness, followed a month later by sluggishness. He presented again in June 2019. On exam his temperature was 38.2 °C, pulse 92 bpm, blood pressure 112/74 mmHg, respirations 18/min; he was conscious but responded slowly. ICP was 150 mmH₂O; CSF protein 4.67 g/L, WBC 68 cells/µL, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.38. “Etiological investigations revealed an unremarkable CSF analysis.” Neurological testing showed slight cognitive decline (MoCA 26, IHDS 8). Brain MRI demonstrated multiple regions of thickened and enhancing meninges.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recurrent cryptococcal meningitis considered but unlikely because repeat CSF India‑ink staining and cultures were negative. | “India ink staining yielded negative results, and the etiological investigation was negative.”
2. New bacterial meningitis deemed improbable given modest CSF pleocytosis, low protein elevation relative to bacterial infection, and preserved CSF glucose ratio. | “CSF protein was 4.67 g/L, CSF WBC was 68 cells/µL, CSF glucose was 1.8 mmol/L, and CSF: serum glucose ratio was 0.38.”
3. IRIS supported by recent immune recovery (CD4 increase from 82 to 132 cells/µL, undetectable HIV load) coinciding with meningeal inflammation on MRI and lack of identifiable pathogen. | “He was re‑admitted with an undetectable viral load and CD4 cell count of 132 cells/µL… Brain MRI revealed multiple regions of thickening and meningeal enhancement… Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with IRIS.”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies acute HIV infection (HIV-1) as the cause of the meningitis. HIV/AIDS is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, therefore the target diagnosis is **hiv_aids**.
2. Breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to the point where cerebrospinal fluid was obtained for metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) but before the mNGS report disclosed HIV‑1 sequences. A 38‑year‑old man with no past medical history was admitted for a 13‑day history of fever, headache, and scattered limb rashes. The fever peaked at 38.5 °C, accompanied by fatigue and headache. Initial routine blood work suggested infection; he received ceftriaxone for 1 week without defervescence, and the rash resolved after self‑administered anti‑allergic medication. One day prior to admission his headache worsened and his response became sluggish, prompting hospitalization.

On examination: blood pressure 125/78 mmHg, temperature 38 °C, pulse 84 bpm, respiration 22/min. He was conscious with slow reaction, negative neck rigidity, pharyngeal hyperemia, no tonsillar swelling, and no cardiac, pulmonary, or abdominal abnormalities. Scattered erythematous macules were present on extremities; no lymphadenopathy, normal muscle strength, and no focal neurologic signs.

Laboratory findings on admission: WBC 10.89 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 37.6 %, lymphocytes 57 %); CRP 0.93 mg/L, PCT 0.13 ng/mL; ALT 148 U/L, AST 106 U/L; HIV antigen/antibody test negative; Chest CT normal.

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 110 mmH₂O; CSF clear, yellowish; nucleated cells 380 /µL (1 % neutrophils, 99 % lymphocytes); glucose 2.0 mmol/L (low); chloride 117.8 mmol/L (low); protein >6000 mg/L (markedly elevated); LDH 161 U/L. Color Doppler ultrasound of cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes, as well as hepatobiliary, pancreatic, and splenic regions, were unremarkable.

Additional tests: blood T‑SPOT (TB) negative; CSF cryptococcal antigen negative; CSF MTB DNA negative; blood and CSF cultures showed no bacterial growth. On hospital day 2, 3 mL of CSF was sent for metagenomic next‑generation sequencing.

Cryptococcus neoformans capsular antigen, fungal (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan, T‑cell assay, GeneXpert for tuberculosis, autoantibodies, and rheumatoid factor were all negative. case_prompt:
A 59‑year‑old previously healthy man, employed in decoration and transportation, developed a sudden, severe, paroxysmal cough with expectoration on 27 October 2021. He sought care at an outpatient clinic; chest computed tomography (CT) revealed multiple patches and nodules with bronchiectasis in both lungs. He was prescribed oral moxifloxacin for three days, but his fever persisted, reaching 39.7 °C, prompting presentation to the emergency department. Repeat chest CT showed progression of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates with bronchiectasis. Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 18.1 × 10⁹/L and a C‑reactive protein (CRP) of 165.7 mg/L; arterial blood gas showed mild hypoxemia (PaO₂ 8.7 kPa). He was admitted.

On examination his pulse was 94/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 102/68 mm Hg, and temperature 40 °C. Lung expansion was symmetric, percussion normal, but breath sounds were reduced in the right lower lung. Cardiac, abdominal, extremity, skin, and neurologic examinations were unremarkable.

Further labs showed mild coagulation and liver function abnormalities, CRP now 185.9 mg/L, leukocytes 21.7 × 10⁹/L with 91.7 % neutrophils (neutrophil count 19.9 × 10⁹/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 62 mm/h, negative Cryptococcus capsular antigen, galactomannan antigen 0.34 µg/L, fungal G test 56 ng/L, immunoglobulin E 1518 IU/mL, and procalcitonin 0.65 µg/L. Autoimmune panels (immunoglobulin, rheumatism, light chain, extractable nuclear antigen, ANCA) were abnormal. Sputum culture and acid‑fast bacilli smear were negative.

Because his fever and pulmonary infiltrates did not improve with moxifloxacin, and the infection appeared to spread rapidly along pulmonary vessels, the team suspected infection with an unusual pathogen, possibly transmitted hematogenously. On further questioning he recalled transporting moldy paper flooring 15 days prior to symptom onset. Empiric therapy with piperacillin‑tazobactam plus moxifloxacin was started, and peripheral blood was sent for quantitative metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (Q‑mNGS).

5. Other fungal infections considered; fungal G test was only modestly elevated (56 ng/L) and did not correlate with typical fungal disease patterns. | "\"fungal G test\" result of 56 ng/L."

case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old Caucasian man was admitted with a 10‑day history of fever, severe headache, and dizziness. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated cryptococcal meningitis. He was also found to have pulmonary tuberculosis and HIV infection, with a CD4 count of 45 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 873,083 copies/mL. Treatment was started with liposomal amphotericin B, fluconazole, and antituberculosis drugs.

Seven weeks later, before antiretroviral therapy was initiated, he reported decreased visual acuity in the right eye and was referred to ophthalmology. There was no prior ocular disease or surgery. Best‑corrected visual acuity was 9/10 in the right eye and 10/10 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination was normal. Dilated fundus examination showed cotton‑wool spots and pre‑ and intraretinal hemorrhages in both eyes. Spectral‑domain OCT revealed inner nuclear layer thinning below the fovea in the parafoveal area of both eyes. OCT‑angiography demonstrated areas of deep capillary plexus ischemia lacking capillaries. Fluorescein angiography identified microaneurysms and late leakage in both eyes. Visual‑field testing documented central scotoma in the right eye and paracentral scotomas in both eyes.

1. Cotton‑wool spots and retinal hemorrhages point toward a microvascular HIV‑related retinopathy rather than necrotizing infectious retinitis. | "Dilated fundus examination revealed cotton‑wool spots and pre‑ and intraretinal hemorrhages in both eyes compatible with HIV retinopathy."
2. Absence of anterior segment inflammation makes anterior uveitis or keratitis unlikely. | "Anterior segment evaluation was unremarkable."
3. Multimodal imaging (OCT thinning, OCTA capillary loss, FA leakage) supports non‑necrotizing microvascular injury consistent with HIV retinopathy and argues against focal infectious lesions such as CMV or toxoplasma, which typically show full‑thickness necrotizing lesions. | (Imaging findings described without mention of necrotizing lesions).

case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old man presented for evaluation of a lung shadow incidentally discovered three weeks earlier on routine physical examination. He denied cough, sputum, dyspnea, fever, chest pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, or appetite changes. Past surgical history was notable for left clavicle fracture repair five years prior; pre‑operative chest X‑ray was normal. He worked as an electric welder for >30 years and had a 20‑year smoking history (10 cigarettes/day), which he quit after the shadow was found.

Vital signs: temperature 36.6 °C, pulse 69/min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 122/82 mmHg. Physical examination was unremarkable; breath sounds were clear with no rales. Routine laboratory tests and ECG were normal. Epigastric ultrasonography showed no relevant abnormality. Pulmonary function testing revealed mild obstructive dysfunction with normal diffusion and a negative bronchodilator response.

Chest CT performed three weeks earlier showed diffuse lesions with localized emphysema, thick‑walled cavities, and multiple nodules in both lungs (both pulmonary and mediastinal windows). Ground‑glass attenuation was interpreted as diffuse alveolar exudation, and, together with his occupational exposure, pneumoconiosis was considered. The authors noted that “welding‑associated pulmonary fibrosis was the most likely diagnosis for this patient,” but proceeded with fiberoptic bronchoscopy for further evaluation.

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was obtained from the posterior segment of the right upper lobe and the lingular segment of the left upper lobe. The right‑lung BAL fluid was bloody‑turbid with 510 cells/µL (60% neutrophils); the left‑lung BAL fluid was clear with 63 cells/µL (6% neutrophils). Staining of BAL fluid revealed macrophages laden with numerous brown‑black particles of varying size, and Prussian blue staining was positive, indicating substantial iron deposition. Electron microscopy demonstrated macrophage cytoplasm containing large, irregular iron particles with metallic luster. The authors emphasized that “the patient's macrophage iron particles differ significantly from those in cases of pulmonary hemorrhage.” CT also demonstrated cavitary lesions with mural nodules and some calcified nodules, raising the consideration of prior tuberculosis.

1. Welding‑associated pulmonary fibrosis was initially favored because of the patient’s long‑term welding exposure and CT findings; however, the presence of iron‑laden macrophages on BAL suggested a different process. | "Although welding‑associated pulmonary fibrosis was the most likely diagnosis for this patient..."
2. Siderosis (iron pneumoconiosis) was supported by BAL and tissue studies showing abundant iron particles with positive Prussian blue staining and characteristic electron‑microscopic appearance. | "Positive Prussian blue staining ... substantial iron particles." and "The St. Regis staining ... macrophages engulfing a large number of brown‑black particles..."
3. Pulmonary hemorrhage was considered but ruled out because the iron particles observed differed in size, color, and refractivity from hemosiderin typical of hemorrhage. | "The patient's macrophage iron particles differ significantly from those in cases of pulmonary hemorrhage..."
4. Old or healed tuberculosis was contemplated based on cavitary lesions with mural nodules and calcifications on CT, but microbiologic confirmation was lacking at this stage. | "considering the possibility of old TB."
5. Active tuberculosis was ultimately confirmed by acid‑fast staining of bronchoscopic brush smears and BAL fluid, which revealed acid‑fast bacilli. | "acid‑fast staining ... showed that acid‑fast bacilli were positive (6 in 300 fields)."

case_prompt:
A 60‑year‑old man with untreated arterial hypertension and a body‑mass index of 28.7 kg/m² was admitted to the intensive‑care unit in March 2020 for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) that had followed a “flu‑like syndrome” over the preceding two weeks. After two weeks of home prednisolone (20 mg/day), his condition worsened, with arterial oxygen saturation dropping to 70 % and requiring emergency ambulance transport. On arrival he was intubated and ventilated prior to ICU transfer.  

At ICU admission his vital signs were: moderate tachycardia (90 bpm), elevated blood pressure (170/80 mm Hg), moderate fever (38.0 °C) and PaO₂ of 120 mm Hg on FiO₂ 1.0 with PEEP 18 cmH₂O. The patient was weaned from VV‑ECMO after 11 days.

COVID‑19 viral pneumonia suspected due to recent flu‑like prodrome, March 2020 pandemic timing, and characteristic alveolo‑interstitial pattern on chest CT. | "A 60‑year‑old man … was admitted … for an ARDS after a ‘flu‑like syndrome’… A chest CT scan showing a major alveolo‑interstitial pneumonia."

case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old man was admitted to the intensive care unit at Steve Biko Academic Hospital with acute pancreatitis, clinically suspected on the basis of a raised amylase level (450 U/L; reference range: 20‑104 U/L) and later confirmed on computed tomography. The pancreatitis was attributed to the use of herbal medication and a cytomegalovirus infection (viral load: 5 472 U/L). The patient was HIV co‑infected (stage 4 WHO) and had not yet started highly active antiretroviral therapy. He also had stage 3 chronic kidney disease, proven on biopsy to be due to HIV‑related focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, complicated by anaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

During admission he developed severe acute hypocalcaemia (corrected serum calcium 1.09 mmol/L; reference range: 2.15‑2.50 mmol/L), precipitated by pancreatitis‑induced saponification and aggressive saline administration. Clinically this manifested as a positive Trousseau’s sign during blood pressure measurement and a prolonged corrected QT interval (QTc 360 ms) on the electrocardiograph.

Twenty‑four hours after admission the patient became unexpectedly unstable, developing acute pulmonary oedema that required mechanical ventilation. An electrocardiogram performed at that time revealed ST‑elevation consistent with an acute myocardial infarction. Initial serum troponin was within the normal range (40 ng/L) but later rose markedly (peak 4 358 ng/L). Urine output remained >1 mL/kg/h.

An acute ST‑elevation myocardial infarction was diagnosed, and a thrombolytic agent was prescribed while intravenous calcium replacement had been initiated as part of his resuscitation.

Serum troponins were initially within the normal range (40 ng/L), but later became markedly elevated (peak: 4 358 ng/L)."

Electrolyte‑induced ST changes due to severe hypocalcaemia were considered given the pronounced hypocalcaemia and associated QTc prolongation | "The patient developed severe, acute hypocalcaemia (corrected serum calcium level: 1.09 mmol/L)... Clinically, this presented as a positive Trousseau’s sign... and a prolonged corrected QT interval (QTc 360 ms)."  
3. Underlying coronary artery disease was ruled out by non‑invasive imaging: technetium sestamibi scan showed no perfusion defects | "A technetium sestamibi scan of the patient's myocardium revealed no perfusion defects."  
4. Coronary calcification or atherosclerotic plaques were excluded on non‑contrast chest CT | "A non‑contrast CT scan of the chest revealed no coronary artery calcification or plaques."  
5. Structural coronary abnormalities were excluded by cardiac MRI, which demonstrated normal coronary arteries without stenosis or bridging myocardium | "A cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan revealed normal coronary arteries, with no areas of stenosis and no bridging myocardium."  
6. Coronary angiography could not be performed because of chronic kidney disease, but the cumulative imaging data made obstructive coronary disease unlikely | "A coronary angiogram was contraindicated owing to the patient's CKD."

case_prompt:
A 9‑year‑old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1‑day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He had been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for a month, with a noticeable increase in pallor a week before admission. On examination he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced; he was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and small palpable lymph nodes in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed anemia (hemoglobin 97 mg/L) and severe thrombocytopenia (platelet 11 × 10⁹/L). White‑blood‑cell count was 10.2 × 10⁹/L with neutrophilic predominance and reactive changes. Reticulocyte count was 2.45 %. Peripheral smear demonstrated red‑cell fragmentation (schistocytes 1.45 %). LDH was markedly elevated at 1,021 U/L; AST 46 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 143 IU/L, total bilirubin 41.3 µmol/L, direct bilirubin 12.7 µmol/L. BUN and creatinine were normal. Urinalysis showed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation studies were normal; fibrinogen was low‑normal at 1.72 g/L; direct Coombs test was negative.

Initial management for presumptive idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (IVIG) failed, and a trial of pulse methylprednisolone also did not improve counts. Bone‑marrow aspiration showed megakaryocytes suggestive of immune destruction; biopsy revealed frequent small epithelioid non‑necrotizing granulomas, a nonspecific finding that can be seen with infections, sarcoidosis, or malignancy.

Viral surveillance (EBV, CMV, HIV) was negative, and QuantiFERON‑TB Gold test was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and chest/abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy. Because brucellosis is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, Brucella serology was sent and returned positive: Brucella abortus 1:5,120 and Brucella melitensis 1:20,480.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) was considered due to isolated thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding, but lack of response to IVIG and steroids made it unlikely. | "Initially, the patient was diagnosed with atypical idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and treated with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg... without response, and his Hgb and platelet counts declined further."
2. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was entertained because of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, elevated LDH) and severe thrombocytopenia, but definitive ADAMTS‑13 results were pending at this stage. | "The final result of BMA revealed peripheral destruction of blood cells, indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), likely TTP, congenital or acquired due to an immune reaction to ADAMTS‑13;"
3. Congenital or immune‑mediated causes of ADAMTS‑13 deficiency were contemplated, yet the clinical course and lack of prior episodes favored an acquired process later confirmed by antibody testing. | (future ADAMTS‑13 data not yet available at the breakpoint)
4. Infectious granulomatous etiologies (viral, bacterial, mycobacterial) were evaluated because bone‑marrow biopsy showed non‑necrotizing granulomas. Viral panel (EBV, CMV, HIV) was negative, and TB screening (QuantiFERON‑TB Gold) was negative, reducing the likelihood of those infections. | "Viral surveillance, including EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative. QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative."
5. Sarcoidosis was a differential for granulomas, but the patient’s age, lack of pulmonary involvement, and epidemiologic context made it less probable. | "Considering that this is a nonspecific finding that could be attributed to various etiologies, including infections (viral, bacterial, and tuberculosis), infiltrating diseases such as sarcoidosis, and malignancies..."
6. Malignancy (leukemia, lymphoma) was considered given cytopenias and splenomegaly, yet bone‑marrow aspiration did not suggest malignancy and imaging showed no significant lymphadenopathy. | "The preliminary report of the BMA did not suggest malignancy; ... Abdominal ultrasound and computerized chest and abdominal tomography (CT) scan showed splenomegaly with no significant lymph node enlargement."
7. Brucellosis was identified as the likely infectious cause because of endemic exposure, recent consumption of unpasteurized goat products, granulomatous marrow changes, and markedly elevated serologic titers for both B. abortus and B. melitensis. | "Since Brucella is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed a significant amount of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, brucella titers were sent, and the result showed Brucella abortus 1:5,120 ... Brucella melitensis 1:20,480."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on drug‑induced interstitial lung disease (DILD) after FOLFIRI + bevacizumab chemotherapy. DILD is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases, so the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.

At this point we have the clinical picture (new ground‑glass opacities, hypoxemia), negative infectious work‑up, and no evidence of radiation pneumonitis or GVHD, allowing the learner to formulate the diagnosis.  
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors excluded bacterial, fungal, pneumocystis, CMV, tuberculosis, radiation‑induced pneumonitis, chronic GVHD, and tumor progression through negative cultures/PCR, normal serologies (KL‑6, β‑D‑glucan), imaging lacking fibrosis, and pathology showing no inflammation. case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man with advanced, BRAF‑mutated colorectal cancer and multiple lung, liver, and peritoneal metastases presented after transverse colostomy for obstructive tumor. He had a remote history of allogeneic bone‑marrow transplantation (33 years prior) with total lymph node irradiation limited to the lung apices and a grade 1 acute GVHD rash that resolved; chronic GVHD was only suspected on skin biopsy. He was not on any immunosuppressants at the time of cancer diagnosis. He received two doses of Moderna COVID‑19 vaccine 9–10 months earlier; PCR tests for SARS‑CoV‑2 were repeatedly negative. Baseline chest CT showed multiple pulmonary nodules but no fibrosis. One month after surgery, first‑line FOLFIRI + bevacizumab chemotherapy was started. On day 6 of cycle 1 he developed a fever without myelosuppression; cultures were negative and a non‑infectious fever resolved with naproxen. He was discharged and received a second chemotherapy cycle as an outpatient without severe adverse events. 

On day 15 of the second cycle, SpO₂ fell to 92 % on room air, prompting admission. Repeat chest CT demonstrated new, slight bilateral ground‑glass shadows without tumor growth. Bronchoscopy showed a normal airway lumen; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) from the middle lobe and a peripheral lung biopsy from the right lower lobe were performed. BAL bacterial and fungal cultures were negative, and PCR for *Pneumocystis jirovecii* and cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA were negative. Lung biopsy revealed metastatic colon cancer but no inflammation. Serum LDH and KL‑6 levels were normal, β‑D‑glucan was negative, and the interferon‑γ release assay for tuberculosis was negative. White‑blood‑cell count was 2,740 /µL (neutrophils 1,140, lymphocytes 880). The differential diagnosis at this stage included interstitial pneumonitis or atypical pneumonia.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered but excluded because “all screening tests including blood cultures for bacterial infections … were negative” and “bacterial culture was negative” on BAL.  
2. Fungal infection excluded as “fungal cultures … were negative” and “beta‑D‑glucan test was negative.”  
3. *Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia ruled out by “PCR tests for pneumocystis jirovecii DNA … were negative.”  
4. CMV pneumonitis excluded initially: “PCR tests for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA of the BAL fluid were negative.”  
5. Tuberculosis excluded with a negative interferon‑gamma release assay: “interferon‑gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative.”  
6. Radiation‑induced pneumonitis deemed unlikely because “no pulmonary changes suggestive of radiation pneumonitis were noted thereafter” and the irradiated field involved only the lung apices, not the current ground‑glass areas.  
7. Chronic GVHD pulmonary involvement ruled out: “There were no apparent clinical manifestations of chronic GVHD around the time of DILD.”  
8. Disease progression (tumor infiltration) considered but imaging showed “no apparent tumor growth” and pathology showed “no obvious fibrosis in the background lungs consistent with the CT findings.”  
9. Atypical pneumonia remained a possibility, yet the lack of infectious evidence and normal inflammatory markers made it less likely, leading the authors to favor an immune‑mediated process.  
10. Drug‑induced interstitial lung disease (DILD) was supported by the temporal relationship to chemotherapy, exclusion of infections and other causes, and the rapid clinical improvement after high‑dose steroids (not yet administered at the breakpoint).

case_prompt:
A 49‑year‑old man from Fuzhou, Fujian Province, presented in April 2019 with a dry cough that began three days earlier, followed by a low‑grade fever (up to 37.7 °C) and exertional dyspnea. He was admitted to the Department of Organ Transplantation two days after fever onset. His past medical history was significant for hypertension, uremia on long‑term peritoneal dialysis, and a renal transplant performed in January 2019. He also reported favism, a penicillin allergy, and denied other medical problems.

On admission his vital signs were: blood pressure 108/71 mm Hg, pulse 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, temperature 37 °C. Physical examination revealed a renal transplant scar on the abdomen without tenderness; the transplanted kidney was non‑tender. Chest CT showed bilateral lung infection, paraseptal emphysema of the upper lobes, and a small pericardial effusion.

Laboratory evaluation demonstrated: 
- Elevated (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan (G test) 325 pg/mL suggesting deep fungal infection,
- Anemia, severe thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia,
- Hepatic and renal dysfunction,
- Immunodeficiency with CD4 count 156 cells/µL and CD8 count 64 cells/µL,
- Positive human cytomegalovirus DNA (HCMV‑DNA),
- Glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase activity 702.2 U/L.

Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus + mycophenolate mofetil) were stopped; antimicrobial therapy (cefoperazone‑tazobactam, micafungin, ganciclovir), immunoglobulin, gastric protection, red‑cell transfusion, cooling and nutritional support were initiated. Two days later a repeat chest CT showed progression of the bilateral lung infection.

A few days later the patient developed severe dyspnea and a fever of 39 °C.

1. Pneumocystis pneumonia considered because of profound CD4 lymphopenia in a recent renal transplant recipient, progressive dyspnea, non‑specific bilateral infiltrates, and lack of response to broad antibacterial/antifungal therapy | "Immunodeficiency (CD4 cells, 156/microL; and CD8 cells, 64/microL)" and "A few days later, the patient developed severe asthma and fever (39 °C)".
2. CMV pneumonitis considered due to positive HCMV‑DNA, but ruled out as sole cause by persistent fever despite ganciclovir and worsening imaging | "human cytomegalovirus infection (HCMV‑DNA positive)" and "the infection aggravated (G test of 1,493 pg/mL)".
3. Bacterial pneumonia initially presumed, treated with cefoperazone‑tazobactam and imipenem, yet imaging showed progression, indicating inadequate coverage for the true pathogen | "anti‑infective regimen ... was changed" after lack of improvement.
4. Candidiasis considered after BAL PCR identified Candida parapsilosis and blood cultures later grew T. marneffei, but these organisms appeared later in the course and did not explain the early deterioration | "Respiratory pathogen detection (bronchoalveolar lavage fluid PCR) showed Candida parapsilosis" and "blood culture returned T. marneffei".
5. Confirmation of Pneumocystis jiroveci by BAL PCR led to targeted therapy with high‑dose sulfamethoxazole, after which the patient’s vital signs stabilized for several days | "Respiratory pathogen detection (bronchoalveolar lavage fluid PCR) suggested Pneumocystis jiroveci."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case culminates in a diagnosis of sulfasalazine‑induced DRESS triggering secondary HLH. Neither DRESS nor HLH appears in the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE. The only SELECTED disease mentioned (COVID‑19) is already diagnosed early and is not the mystery to be solved. Therefore, final diagnosis will be “DRESS -> OUT_OF_SCOPE”.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to the point just before the authors explicitly state the RegiSCAR score and the diagnosis of DRESS. This provides the patient’s presentation, laboratory abnormalities, imaging findings, and negative infectious/autoimmune work‑up, allowing the learner to infer a severe drug reaction with systemic involvement without revealing the label.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors used (a) temporal relation to sulfasalazine initiation, (b) multi‑system involvement (fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, hyperferritinemia), (c) high RegiSCAR score, and (d) exclusion of infections and malignancy (negative cultures, PET‑CT, bone‑marrow) to confirm DRESS, while the fulfillment of ≥5 HLH criteria (ferritin, triglycerides, cytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, cytokine storm) supported secondary HLH.
case_prompt:
A 36‑year‑old Chinese man with ankylosing spondylitis had started sulfasalazine one month earlier. Two weeks after initiation he developed high fever (up to 40 °C), facial swelling, generalized erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Empiric antibiotics (ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, levofloxacin) at a local hospital failed to improve his condition. Laboratory evaluation showed marked leukocytosis (228.9 ×10⁹/L), elevated aspartate aminotransferase (324 U/L) and alanine aminotransferase (114 U/L), and a high B‑type natriuretic peptide (1411 pg/mL). COVID‑19 PCR was positive, and he was diagnosed with drug hypersensitivity syndrome, drug‑induced liver injury, and COVID‑19 infection. He received methylprednisolone 160 mg/day, intravenous immunoglobulin 32.5 g/day, and a 5‑day course of Paxlovid, after which fever and rash subsided. He was transferred for further care.

On examination, a diffuse exanthematous eruption was noted on the trunk. Methylprednisolone was tapered every 3–5 days, leading to resolution of skin lesions and normalization of leukocyte count, transaminases, and BNP. Five days later he abruptly redeveloped high fever (up to 40 °C) with abdominal pain. New laboratory abnormalities included: serum ferritin 11 895 ng/mL, fibrinogen 1.02 g/L, procalcitonin 0.61 ng/mL, ALT 2462 IU/L, AST 1191 IU/L, ESR 109 mm/h, CRP 145 mg/L, triglycerides 9.79 mmol/L, NK‑cell count 32 cells/µL, and markedly elevated cytokines (IL‑2, IL‑2R, IL‑6, IL‑8, IL‑10, IFN‑γ). Autoimmune serology revealed negative ANCA and rheumatoid factor, positive antinuclear antibodies (1:1000 speckled), anti‑U1‑snRNP (23.9 AI) and anti‑SS‑A (22.7 AI). EBV DNA was 4.11 × 10⁵ copies/mL and CMV DNA 3.73 × 10³ copies/mL. Thyroid studies showed low T3, free T3, T4, free T4, and thyroglobulin, with elevated anti‑thyroglobulin and anti‑thyroid peroxidase antibodies.

Abdominal CT demonstrated heterogeneous liver densities suggestive of intra‑hepatic lymphatic congestion, a possible liver cyst, an edematous enlarged gallbladder, splenomegaly, irregular kidneys with thickened fascia, a non‑compressible 11‑mm appendix surrounded by hazy fat, and a small pelvic fluid collection. PET‑CT showed no definitive malignancy. Axillary ultrasonography revealed several lymph nodes without increased internal vascular flow. Bone‑marrow biopsy was negative for malignancy and showed no hemophagocytosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Temporal relationship to sulfasalazine suggests a drug‑induced reaction | "According to the Naranjo adverse drug reaction probability scale, it was probably that sulfasalazine induced this condition."
2. Multisystem involvement (fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, hyperferritinemia) fits DRESS criteria | "The RegiSCAR score was determined to be 7, supporting the diagnosis of DRESS."
3. High ferritin, low fibrinogen, hypertriglyceridemia, cytopenia (NK‑cell depletion), and cytokine storm meet HLH diagnostic thresholds | "Our patient fulfilled seven out of the eight required criteria for HLH."
4. Infectious causes less likely: antibiotics ineffective, blood cultures not reported, PET‑CT negative for malignancy, and viral PCRs (EBV, CMV) showed low‑level reactivation only | "Tests for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody and rheumatoid factor yielded negative results, as did serological tests for hepatitis viruses and HIV."
5. COVID‑19 infection present but cannot fully explain the marked hyperferritinemia and severe hepatic injury | "Positive COVID‑19 PCR results. The patient was diagnosed with … COVID‑19 infection."
6. Autoimmune connective‑tissue disease considered (positive ANA, anti‑U1‑snRNP, anti‑SS‑A) but does not account for the abrupt fever spikes and dramatic laboratory derangements | "Concurrent diagnoses of undifferentiated connective tissue disease … were also made."
7. Drug‑induced liver injury alone would not explain the systemic hyperinflammation, lymphadenopathy, and skin eruption | "The patient was diagnosed with drug hypersensitivity syndrome, drug‑induced liver injury, and COVID‑19 infection."
8. Malignancy ruled out by PET‑CT and bone‑marrow biopsy | "PET‑CT scans did not reveal any definitive evidence of malignancy… bone marrow biopsy findings were negative for malignancy."

Best breakpoint: Include the presentation from initial fever and prior treatments through the extensive infectious, autoimmune, and drug‑toxicity work‑up (cultures, imaging, laboratory panels) but stop before the sentence “sintilimab‑induced agranulocytosis was diagnosed” and before the therapeutic plan for G‑CSF and steroids is described. case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man with a history of right‑lung squamous cell carcinoma (cT3N3M0, stage IIIC) and five‑year deep venous thrombosis presented on October 5, 2021 with a one‑month history of recurrent fever and a three‑day history of chest pain. He had been a 40‑pack‑year smoker. Initial therapy at a local hospital began on August 27 with sintilimab (200 mg) plus paclitaxel liposomes (240 mg) and carboplatin (0.45 g). Five days after the first cycle he developed fever up to 40.5 °C; laboratory testing showed grade 3 neutropenia (WBC 1.7 × 10⁹/L, ANC 0.64 × 10⁹/L). Despite granulocyte‑colony stimulating factor (G‑CSF) and a cephalosporin, fever persisted. Blood cultures grew human herpesvirus 5 (HHV‑5), Staphylococcus aureus, and Corynebacterium equi, interpreted as sepsis, and teicoplanin therapy led to clinical improvement and normalization of WBC and ANC.

He was discharged after a second dose of sintilimab and oral edoxaban on September 25. On September 26 he again developed fever (peak 40 °C). At presentation on September 30, WBC and ANC were normal, but C‑reactive protein (42.2 mg/L) and procalcitonin (12.27 ng/mL) were markedly elevated, and antibiotics failed to control the fever.

On admission to our hospital his vital signs were within normal limits; physical examination revealed decreased breath sounds over the left lung. Tumor markers were: CEA 4.49 ng/mL, CYFRA 21‑1 7.22 ng/mL (↑), NSE 15.86 ng/mL, CA‑125 12.41 U/mL, CA‑153 31.40 U/mL (↑). Repeat chest CT on October 5 showed a 6.1 × 5.2 cm mass in the right lower lobe posterior basal segment with mild perilesional inflammation, raising concern for tumor progression.

After six days of anticoagulation and coronary angiography (which excluded coronary artery disease), a third treatment cycle (carboplatin, paclitaxel liposome, bevacizumab, sintilimab) was administered. Shortly after midnight the patient developed fever 40.2 °C and agranulocytosis (WBC 1.3 × 10⁹/L, ANC 0 × 10⁹/L). His leukocyte count continued to fall, reaching a nadir of 0.5 × 10⁹/L on October 16, with persistent ANC 0 × 10⁹/L; hemoglobin also declined from October 13 to 21. Digital radiography on October 13 confirmed the prior CT findings.

Extensive evaluation was undertaken: blood cultures, liver function tests, bacterial cultures, and drug‑toxicity assessment; autoimmune screening showed negative anti‑nuclear antibody and fungal galactomannan; CMV DNA, G test, and renal profile were within normal limits. Sputum culture on October 18 grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The patient had no prior history of agranulocytosis and ANC had been normal throughout earlier cancer treatment. The rapid marrow suppression occurring within 24 h of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and anti‑angiogenic therapy was atypical for classic chemotherapy‑induced nadir. A multidisciplinary team reviewed the data and considered various etiologies before reaching a provisional diagnosis.

A 50‑year‑old man with no prior medical conditions was admitted for COVID‑19 pneumonia. Despite glucocorticoid therapy, his respiratory status worsened, requiring mechanical ventilation on day 7 and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation on day 9. He improved, underwent tracheostomy on day 20, and was transferred for rehabilitation. On day 43 after symptom onset he developed watery diarrhea, which escalated to 6,000–7,000 mL/day after transfer, prompting readmission on day 62.

On admission he was afebrile (36.5 °C), tachycardic (117 bpm), and normotensive (120/83 mm Hg). His weight had fallen from 114.5 kg (BMI 36.5 kg/m²) to 94.6 kg. Stool testing was negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin A/B and glutamate dehydrogenase, and cultures were negative for pathogenic E. coli and C. difficile. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy demonstrated duodenal villous enlargement and ring‑like erosions; capsule endoscopy showed ring‑shaped ulcerations throughout the small bowel; colonoscopy revealed extensive mucosal edema with shallow map‑like ulcerations. Biopsy of colonic and small‑bowel mucosa showed regenerative epithelial changes, inflammatory infiltrates, nuclear inclusion bodies, and immunohistochemistry positive for cytomegalovirus antigen. Blood testing was positive for CMV pp65 antigen (7 positive per 100,000 WBCs). A PCR assay for SARS‑CoV‑2 on colonic tissue was negative. No histologic evidence of vasculitis, thrombus, or inflammatory bowel disease was seen. He was diagnosed with CMV enterocolitis and started on ganciclovir on hospital day 5, but the diarrhea persisted without improvement.

case_prompt:
A 75‑year‑old woman, a farmer with a history of COVID‑19 infection, hypertension, and nephrotic syndrome, was admitted for a prolonged cough, expectoration, fever, and dyspnea. She had been on long‑term steroids (methylprednisolone 40 mg daily) and other chronic medications. On arrival she was febrile (36.3 °C), tachycardic (115 bpm), tachypneic (25 /min) and hypotensive (95/58 mmHg). Physical examination showed pale skin, scattered petechiae, mild lower‑extremity edema, and coarse breath sounds with crackles bilaterally. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (4.77 × 10⁹/L) with neutrophilia (85.8 %), markedly elevated CRP (51.83 mg/L) and procalcitonin (2.60 ng/mL), prolonged prothrombin time, severe anemia (Hb 55 g/L), low total protein (53.1 g/L) and albumin (31.9 g/L), and profound CD4⁺ (224 cells/µL) and CD8⁺ (168 cells/µL) lymphopenia. Chest CT demonstrated diffuse pulmonary inflammation with minimal pleural effusion. Empiric therapy with meropenem, sulfamethoxazole, and caspofungin was started.

On hospital day 2 the patient continued to spike fevers (max 38.9 °C) with rising CRP (88.71 mg/L) and D‑dimer (15.61 mg/L). Broad respiratory pathogen panels (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, rifampicin‑resistance gene, acid‑fast smear, Streptococcus pneumoniae antigen, Influenza A/B, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Aspergillus antigen, Cryptococcus neoformans antigen) were all negative. Because initial tests failed to identify a pathogen, metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and blood was performed.

mNGS of BALF identified large numbers of reads corresponding to Enterococcus faecium, Candida albicans, Candida glabrata, Strongyloides stercoralis, and Human Parainfluenza Virus Type 3. Blood mNGS detected Strongyloides stercoralis (15 reads). Conventional blood culture grew Enterococcus faecium (susceptible to vancomycin and linezolid) and sputum culture grew moderate Candida glabrata. Additional laboratory testing revealed Epstein‑Barr virus DNA (1.26 × 10³ copies/mL), cytomegalovirus DNA (8.19 × 10³ copies/mL), and (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan (119.58 pg/mL). Re‑examination of the BALF smear showed numerous Gram‑positive cocci, fungal spores, pseudohyphae, and, on repeated microscopic examination, Strongyloides stercoralis larvae. Stool specimens could not be obtained because the patient did not defecate during hospitalization.

Bacterial pneumonia (Enterococcus faecium) considered because of leukocytosis, elevated procalcitonin, and positive blood culture; however, Enterococcus is a typical gut flora and may represent colonization or secondary infection rather than primary cause | "blood culture indicated the presence of Enterococcus faecium, and the in vitro drug susceptibility test demonstrated sensitivity to vancomycin and linezolid."

Fungal pneumonia (Candida spp.) suggested by high (1,3)-β‑D‑glucan and growth of Candida glabrata in sputum; yet Candida is often a colonizer of airways and did not explain the severe clinical picture alone | "sputum culture disclosed moderate growth of Candida glabrata" and "(1,3)-beta-D-glucan at a level of 119.58 pg./mL."

Based on the patient’s history and findings, hematologic diseases, immune system disorders, and KFD were considered as potential diagnoses.

A 28‑year‑old man from Cuba, residing in Spain for six months, presented after a 3‑week history of fever, diarrhea, and abdominal pain and was diagnosed with HIV infection (CD4+ count 14 cells/μL, HIV‑1 RNA 4.2 × 10⁶ copies/mL). He reported sexual exposure as the transmission route and had no significant past medical history except former smoking. Before starting antiretroviral therapy, he was evaluated for opportunistic infections but results were pending when he developed a 4‑day history of rapid‑onset dry cough and somnolence, prompting an emergency‑room visit.

On examination he was febrile (39 °C), tachycardic (120 bpm), and tachypneic (22 rpm) with oxygen saturation 99 % on room air. He appeared dehydrated, had mild hepatomegaly (1 cm), and lung and neurological exams were unremarkable. Chest X‑ray showed subtle bilateral interstitial infiltrates.

CT of the chest demonstrated extensive bilateral ground‑glass opacities, some with a pseudo‑nodular pattern and a left‑lower‑lobe cavitary lesion. Empiric broad‑spectrum antimicrobials (including cotrimoxazole and foscarnet) and high‑dose methylprednisolone were started because of a high HScore (286) suggesting secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. He progressed to severe ARDS (PaO₂/FiO₂ = 60 mmHg) and was placed on veno‑venous ECMO.

Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was excluded by negative antigen testing and NAAT on bronchoalveolar samples. Disseminated histoplasmosis was ruled out by negative fungal cultures. Tuberculosis and non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection were excluded by negative cultures and NAATs from respiratory, blood, bone‑marrow, urine, and stool specimens.

She had received a 7‑day course of levofloxacin for presumed right‑lung pneumonia without improvement. Bronchoscopy revealed friable, bleeding, irregular mucosa of the right upper lobe entry; biopsies were not feasible. Ziehl‑Neelsen and auramine stains of the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were negative and cytology was normal. Thoracic CT showed atelectasis caused by an 8 × 7 cm irregular mass obstructing the right superior lobar bronchus with multiple mediastinal and hilar adenopathies.  

Because a neoplastic process was most likely, she was discharged to await a scheduled transthoracic biopsy. A BAL culture later grew acid‑fast bacilli, prompting readmission for evaluation of active tuberculosis. On admission she was afebrile, vital signs normal, with reduced vesicular breath sounds over the right lung. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis 26 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 21 × 10⁹/L, lymphocytes 3 × 10⁹/L), hemoglobin 71 g/L (MCV 73 fL), platelets 766 × 10⁹/L, CRP 111 mg/L, ESR 25 mm/h, procalcitonin 19 µg/L. PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex on sputum was negative. She subsequently developed fever with purulent sputum and was started on piperacillin‑tazobactam for post‑obstructive pneumonia.  

Endobronchial ultrasound showed purulent secretions and a narrowed right superior lobar bronchus; transbronchial needle aspirations of mediastinal nodes were performed. Two days later she required ICU transfer; vancomycin was added. White‑cell count rose to 47 × 10⁹/L and chest X‑ray demonstrated new right‑lower‑lobe and middle‑lobe infiltrates with a large pleural effusion. Pleural fluid was an exudate with lymphocytic predominance. She required intubation and vasopressors for septic shock. Mediastinoscopy biopsies and transthoracic biopsy of the mass showed only fibrosis and nonspecific reactive lymphoid infiltrates, without granulomas.  

On ICU day 8, the original BAL isolate was identified as Mycobacterium colombiense by 16S rRNA sequencing. Susceptibility testing showed clarithromycin MIC 0.25 mg/L (susceptible) while rifampin MIC was 4 mg/L and ethambutol MIC > 16 mg/L. Treatment with rifampicin, clarithromycin, and ethambutol was initiated. The patient’s course was complicated by multiresistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa cultured from mediastinoscopy specimens; antibiotic regimens were sequentially adjusted (doripenem/tobramycin, then piperacillin‑tazobactam, ciprofloxacin). Despite transient stability, recurrent P. aeruginosa isolation from tracheal aspirates led to renewed therapy.  

On the final bronchoscopy, cultures grew cytomegalovirus in fibroblast cell culture many days later, and CMV inclusions were later identified in lung, mediastinal nodes, thyroid, pancreas, and adrenal glands. The patient died on ICU day 34 from septic shock with multiorgan failure.
