case_prompt:
A 63‑year‑old woman with mixed connective tissue disease, interstitial lung disease, severe pulmonary hypertension, and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was admitted for a one‑day history of jaundice and a two‑week history of malaise and confusion. Her rheumatologic regimen had been azathioprine and prednisone; six weeks earlier her prednisone dose was increased from 2 mg daily to 40 mg daily for worsening myositis. One month after this increase she developed worsening pedal edema and large bullae on both lower extremities that ruptured, leaving ulcerations. Two weeks later her family noted increasing confusion and somnolence and brought her to the emergency department.

On admission: temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 124/98 mmHg, pulse 69 /min, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO₂ 97 % on room air. Physical exam showed marked scleral icterus, jaundice, diffuse abdominal tenderness, a non‑verbal state, and two symmetric, well‑circumscribed shallow ulcerations on the medial aspects of both lower legs.

Laboratory studies: WBC 900 /µL (82 % neutrophils, ANC 700), hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, platelets 155 × 10³/µL; AST 83 U/L, ALT 144 U/L; total bilirubin 24.2 mg/dL; INR 8.8 (on chronic warfarin); serum ammonia 42 µg/dL; urinalysis with mild proteinuria and 11–25 leukocytes/hpf. Blood cultures grew aerobic gram‑negative rods in two consecutive bottles. Abdominal ultrasound showed cholelithiasis without biliary dilation; CT abdomen demonstrated a small enhancing lesion in the medial segment of the left hepatic lobe.

Initial impression: septicemia, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, and neutropenia. She was started on ceftazidime, ciprofloxacin, and lactulose; warfarin was held, azathioprine stopped, and prednisone tapered. Hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B and C PCR, anti‑mitochondrial antibody, and anti‑smooth muscle antibody were all negative.

During the hospital course her liver enzymes remained elevated, mental status worsened with occasional unresponsive episodes, and right‑heart failure with systemic congestion developed. Brain MRI and EEG were unrevealing. The gram‑negative rod was later identified as extended‑spectrum‑β‑lactamase producing Escherichia coli, prompting a change to meropenem.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sepsis from ESBL E. coli considered because of positive blood cultures and abdominal infection risk; excluded as sole cause after lack of improvement with appropriate antibiotics and persistent hepatic dysfunction. | "The gram negative rod was eventually speciated as extended‑spectrum‑beta‑lactamase (ESBL) Escherichia coli, so the antibiotic regimen was switched to meropenem."  
2. Drug‑induced liver injury from azathioprine or high‑dose prednisone considered given immunosuppression and known hepatotoxicity; excluded as liver enzymes and bilirubin remained high despite cessation of these agents and negative viral hepatitis serologies. | "Azathioprine was stopped due to concern of causing bone marrow suppression and contributing to hepatic toxicity."  
3. Cholestasis secondary to cholelithiasis considered because ultrasound showed gallstones; excluded by absence of biliary dilation and lack of response to supportive care. | "Abdominal ultrasound showed cholelithiasis without biliary dilation."  
4. Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C) considered; excluded by negative serologies and PCR. | "Hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B and C polymerase chain reaction (PCR)... all returning negative."  
5. Hepatic encephalopathy from liver failure considered; while present, it did not explain the ulcerative skin lesions nor the marked neutropenia. | "Brain magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography were performed, which did not explain the etiology of encephalopathy."  
6. CMV infection/reactivation considered because of profound neutropenia, ulcerative skin lesions with characteristic histology, and high viral load; confirmed by quantitative PCR, serology, and immunohistochemistry, and rapid clinical response to ganciclovir. | "CMV DNA PCR of serum returned with 173,953 copies... The patient was started on IV ganciclovir... Subsequently, the patient had rapid and marked improvement in laboratory markers and mentation."

case_prompt:
A 58‑year‑old man with end‑stage renal disease had undergone three kidney transplants (1979, 1981, 2008). The most recent transplant was complicated by acute rejection, for which he received anti‑thymoglobulin, plasma exchanges, rituximab, mycophenolate mofetil 1 g/d, tacrolimus 4.5 mg/d, and prednisone 10 mg/d. His past medical history also included chronic hepatitis B, prior legionellosis, chronic Q fever, and cytomegalovirus infection.

In August 2009, after plasma exchanges and high‑dose corticosteroids for graft rejection, he developed fever, anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL) and leukopenia (1 600 cells/µL). Quantitative PCR of blood demonstrated 431 organisms per mL. Liposomal amphotericin B (L‑AmB) induction (total dose 40 mg/kg) improved his condition and reduced the organism load to 6.9 / mL.

A second recurrence occurred in January 2010 with fever and an organism load of 29.6 / mL while on monthly maintenance L‑AmB (3 mg/kg). High‑dose L‑AmB was readministered, followed by a four‑month course of miltefosine. Parasitemia fell to 0.4 / mL and CD4⁺ lymphocyte count rose from 87 to 147 cells/µL.

A third relapse in July 2010 presented with fever, organism load 29.8 / mL, and a positive culture from venous blood. L‑AmB was re‑introduced, then given as maintenance infusions every three weeks for four months, with gradual reduction of immunosuppressive therapy. Persisting symptoms led to weekly, then twice‑weekly, infusions. Parasitemia decreased from 88 to 0.6 / mL, but a fourth recurrence emerged between April and June 2011, marked by fever, leukopenia (1 200 cells/µL, CD4 186 cells/µL), anemia (Hb 9.1 g/dL) and organism load 40 / mL. The patient declined a higher L‑AmB dose; therapy continued at 3 mg/kg twice‑weekly.

In November 2011, the transplanted kidney was removed and chronic dialysis reinstated. By February 2012, he manifested fever, splenomegaly, anemia (Hb 8.6 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 50 × 10³/µL), and markedly elevated organism loads: 12 870 / mL in blood and 60 440 / mL in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. Liver function tests remained normal; ECG showed T‑wave inversion but troponin was normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recurrent fever, cytopenias, and splenomegaly in a heavily immunosuppressed transplant recipient suggest opportunistic infection vs. graft‑rejection–related inflammation. | "In August 2009... fever, anemia... and leukopenia... were observed."
2. Prior history of legionellosis and chronic Q fever raised suspicion for bacterial relapse, but repeated cultures and PCR failed to detect these organisms during the episodes. | "He had previous chronic hepatitis B, legionellosis, chronic Q fever and cytomegalovirus infection."
3. Cytomegalovirus reactivation is common post‑transplant, yet CMV PCR was not reported as positive during the recurrences, and antiviral therapy was not administered. | "He had ... cytomegalovirus infection." (absence of CMV detection during relapses)
4. Acute graft rejection could produce fever and anemia, but the timing of episodes (after immunosuppression intensification) and persistent organism detection favored infectious etiology. | "Relapse occurred... when plasma exchanges and corticosteroids boluses were administered for the graft rejection."
5. The quantitative PCR revealing high organism loads in blood (e.g., 431 / mL, 29.6 / mL, 88 / mL) and bronchoalveolar lavage (60 440 / mL) directly indicated a parasitic bloodstream infection. | "431 Leishmania per ml of blood... 40 Leishmania/ml... 60,440 Leishmania/ml of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid."
6. Response to liposomal amphotericin B and later to meglumine antimoniate—agents specific for Leishmania—supported leishmaniasis as the causative pathogen. | "L‑AmB ... provided improvement... Meglumine antimoniate ... administered daily for 28 days..."
7. Other protozoal infections (e.g., Toxoplasma, Trypanosoma) were not identified by serology or PCR, and the clinical picture (splenomegaly, pancytopenia) aligns with visceral leishmaniasis. | "Leishmania PCR in blood was positive" (implied specificity).

case_prompt:
The patient received a deceased‑donor renal transplant on July 14, 2012. Induction immunosuppression included intravenous basiliximab, and maintenance therapy comprised cyclosporine, mycophenolate, and prednisolone. Early graft function recovered without dialysis; serum creatinine was 2.6 mg/dL at 1 week and 1.2 mg/dL at 1 month with a blood pressure of 110/80 mm Hg off antihypertensives. Cyclosporine trough levels ranged from 142 to 245 ng/mL. He was given valganciclovir for 8 weeks and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.

One month post‑transplant he reported an oral aphthous ulcer that resolved spontaneously. At 3 months (October 5, 2012) he developed low‑grade fever and a rise in serum creatinine from 1.2 to 1.4 mg/dL. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) testing was positive (PP65 antigen 46 × 2/10⁵; PCR 205 copies/mL). Intravenous ganciclovir was started. Ten days later he was admitted with gross hematuria; urine culture grew Klebsiella and was treated with antibiotics. Urinalysis showed numerous RBCs, 2+ albumin, and a 24‑hour protein excretion of 5.3 g/day. Ganciclovir was discontinued after 14 days due to neutropenia, and CMV PCR subsequently became negative. Mycophenolate was switched to azathioprine. During this period he experienced recurrent oral ulcers and a large genital ulcer present for several days.

Two weeks after discharge (November 9, 2012) serum creatinine increased to 1.6 mg/dL, prompting a renal allograft biopsy. Histology revealed three glomeruli with increased mesangial matrix and cellularity, focal neutrophilic infiltration, thin basement membranes, mild patchy interstitial mononuclear infiltrates, and acute tubular necrosis. Immunofluorescence showed abundant peripheral and mesangial C3c deposits and mild IgM deposition; C4d stain was negative. Electron microscopy demonstrated hump‑shaped electron‑dense subepithelial and mesangial deposits without subendothelial deposits. Serum complement C3 was low (<16.9 mg/dL; normal 80–156 mg/dL) with normal C4. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing was negative. Urine PCR for BK virus was negative.

A biopsy of the oral ulcer displayed subepithelial vascular proliferation with perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and scattered neutrophils, consistent with vasculitis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. CMV‑associated glomerulonephritis considered because of recent CMV viremia; excluded by absence of viral inclusions on renal biopsy and negative CMV PCR after treatment. | "No viral inclusions were seen on the biopsy... CMV PCR was negative."
2. BK virus nephropathy considered in transplant recipients; excluded by negative BK virus PCR in urine. | "Urine for BK virus was negative by PCR."
3. Calcineurin‑inhibitor nephrotoxicity considered given cyclosporine use; excluded because biopsy showed immune‑complex deposits (C3c, IgM) and vasculitic changes rather than typical arteriolar hyalinosis or tubular atrophy. | "Immunofluorescence study showed abundant peripheral and mesangial deposits of C3c... The final conclusion was neutrophilic glomerulitis, mesangial proliferation..."
4. ANCA‑associated vasculitis considered due to glomerulonephritis and vasculitic lesions; excluded by negative ANCA testing. | "Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody was negative."
5. Lupus nephritis considered because of low C3 and immune deposits; excluded by lack of full‑house immunofluorescence (IgG, IgA, C1q) and absence of clinical SLE features. | "Immunofluorescence study showed abundant peripheral and mesangial deposits of C3c and mild deposit of IgM... Serum C4 was normal."
6. Infectious endocarditis‑related immune‑complex GN considered; excluded by negative blood cultures and lack of systemic infectious signs. | (Implied by absence of fever and negative cultures in the report.)

case_prompt:
A 59‑year‑old Indian female presented with a two‑month history of abdominal distension, generalized weakness, productive cough, purpuric rashes over both lower limbs, and a two‑day fever. Past medical history included hypertension, hypothyroidism, cholecystectomy 17 years ago, and a recent diagnosis of chronic liver disease secondary to autoimmune hepatitis for which she had been receiving prednisone 60 mg daily for three months and azathioprine 100 mg daily for one month.

On examination she was conscious, oriented, afebrile, pale, with pedal edema and palpable purpuric spots on the lower limbs. Blood pressure was low (80/50 mm Hg) with a pulse of 118/min and respiratory rate of 20/min. Chest examination revealed bilateral normal air entry with basal crepitations. Abdomen was distended, tender, with sluggish bowel sounds.

Laboratory studies showed anemia (Hb 9.3 g/dL), neutrophilia (83 % neutrophils, 11 % lymphocytes, 1 % eosinophils), platelets 139 × 10⁹/L, elevated urea (120 mg/dL) and creatinine (2.08 mg/dL), mild hyponatremia (133 mmol/L), total bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, AST 98 IU/L, ALT 82 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 519 IU/L, GGT 800 IU/L, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 3.3 g/dL, and C‑reactive protein 144 mg/L. Arterial blood gas demonstrated respiratory acidosis (pH 7.30, HCO₃⁻ 20 mm Hg, pCO₂ 46 mm Hg, PO₂ 87 mm Hg) with lactate 3.2 mmol/L. She required intubation and mechanical ventilation due to worsening respiratory status and altered sensorium, and had paralytic ileus with high nasogastric aspirate (600 mL/24 h).

Chest X‑ray showed bilateral fluffy alveolar opacities with infiltrates, left‑side consolidation and right‑sided homogeneous ground‑glass opacities. Echocardiography was unremarkable with an ejection fraction of 50 % and no regional wall motion abnormalities. Abdominal ultrasound revealed an irregular, coarse liver, minimal ascites, and dilated small‑bowel loops with sluggish peristalsis.

Bronchoalveolar lavage cytology demonstrated benign respiratory epithelial cells, a few polymorphs and histiocytes on a hemorrhagic background. Cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae; other cultures were sterile. CMV DNA quantification was 1.81 × 10⁶ copies/mL. Absolute eosinophil count was 55 cells/µL (reference 40–440) and serum IgE 319 IU/mL (reference ≤100). Skin biopsy showed occasional thrombi in dermal vessels with red‑cell extravasation, compatible with purpura fulminans; no larvae were seen.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia/sepsis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae was considered because BAL culture grew this organism, but the extensive pulmonary infiltrates, gastrointestinal ileus, and lack of clinical improvement despite targeted antibiotics suggested an additional process. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. Other cultures were sterile."
2. Cytomegalovirus reactivation was evaluated given the high viral load, yet CMV alone does not explain the cutaneous purpura, paralytic ileus, and motile larvae observed later. | "CMV DNA quant 1.81 x 10⁶/ml."
3. Drug‑induced vasculitis/purpura fulminans was a differential because of purpuric rash and histology showing thrombi, but the skin biopsy did not reveal any parasitic elements and systemic findings were disproportionate. | "Skin biopsy showed occasional thrombi in dermal vessels with extravasation of red blood cells; epidermis was largely unremarkable which is compatible with purpura fulminans. No larvae were seen."
4. Strongyloides stercoralis hyperinfection syndrome was identified as the unifying diagnosis after microscopy revealed motile larvae in the bronchoalveolar lavage, correlating with immunosuppression from high‑dose steroids, gastrointestinal dysmotility, and multi‑organ involvement. | "A wet mount was seen which revealed motile larvae resembling larvae of Strongyloides stercoralis."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The infant harbored Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, which is listed as “pneumocystis” among the 21 SELECTED diseases. This infection is sufficiently documented in the report to be diagnosed before the breakpoint, making it the primary target diagnosis.
2. Best breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to and including the bronchoalveolar lavage PCR results that identified Pneumocystis jirovecii (and CMV) and the imaging finding of interstitial pneumonitis, but stop before the paragraph describing the antimicrobial therapy. This provides enough information for the learner to deduce Pneumocystis pneumonia without revealing the treatment or confirming statement.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated Pneumocystis pneumonia from other opportunistic infections (CMV, bacterial sepsis) by demonstrating PCR detection in BAL, correlating with interstitial pneumonitis on thoracic imaging, and noting the patient’s profound immunodeficiency (hypogammaglobulinemia, low NK/B‑memory cells). They excluded adenoviral gastroenteritis as the cause of pulmonary disease and considered secondary HLH as a systemic process rather than a primary pulmonary pathogen.
case_prompt: A 3‑month‑old male infant presented with persistent diarrhea and failure to thrive. He was born at term to healthy non‑consanguineous Italian parents after an uncomplicated pregnancy. At admission his temperature was 38 °C. Laboratory studies showed a C‑reactive protein of 41 mg/L, white‑blood‑cell count 34.6 × 10³/µL (neutrophils 14.11 × 10³/µL, lymphocytes 15.43 × 10³/µL) and hypereosinophilia (3.8 × 10³/µL). Adenovirus was detected in his stool sample. Physical examination revealed mild dysmorphic features with frontal bossing, micrognathia, hypoplastic nasal wings, flattened alveolar margins, fine sparse hair, absent eyebrows, thin translucent skin with dry eczema and hyperkeratosis. Skin biopsy confirmed absence of sweat glands, consistent with anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. Radiographs demonstrated a “bone‑in‑bone” appearance of the femoral, iliac and ischial bones bilaterally, consistent with osteopetrosis. His condition rapidly deteriorated with dyspnea, oliguria, lethargy and acute seizures; head CT was negative and he was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. On ICU admission leukocytosis rose to 52.24 × 10³/µL and he met criteria for secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia with Hb 6.9 g/dL, ferritin 37 300 ng/mL, LDH 2105 U/L, fibrinogen 93 mg/dL, triglycerides 700 mg/dL). Thoracic imaging showed interstitial pneumonitis. Bronchoalveolar lavage PCR identified Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus DNA.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Adenoviral gastroenteritis was considered because “Adenovirus was detected in his stool sample,” but it does not explain the interstitial pneumonitis and respiratory failure. 
2. Cytomegalovirus pneumonia was a possibility given the detection of viral DNA, as stated: “CMV DNA were identified in the bronchoalveolar lavage by PCR,” yet the concurrent identification of another pathogen required further distinction. 
3. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is most consistent with the interstitial pattern on thoracic imaging and the immunocompromised state, supported by the finding: “Pneumocystis jirovecii … identified in the bronchoalveolar lavage by PCR.” 
4. Bacterial sepsis was entertained, prompting empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics (“He was successfully treated with meropenem…”), but no bacterial organism was isolated from respiratory specimens. 
5. Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis accounted for systemic inflammation: “signs of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with prolonged fever, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia… elevated ferritinemia… low fibrinogen and hypertriglyceridemia.” However, HLH does not pinpoint the specific pulmonary pathogen. 
6. Underlying primary immunodeficiency (IKBKG mutation) predisposed to opportunistic infections, evidenced by “severe hypogammaglobulinemia” and “low NK and B memory cell counts,” guiding the differential toward opportunistic organisms such as Pneumocystis and CMV.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately received a diagnosis of confirmed invasive aspergillosis, which is listed among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore, the target diagnosis is **aspergillosis** (SELECTED).
2. Best Breakpoint: End the case presentation immediately before the authors state “These data indicated a diagnosis of confirmed invasive aspergillosis.” All clinical, radiologic, and microbiologic data that allow a learner to infer invasive aspergillosis (new septic shock, chest CT with nodules, fungal filaments in abscesses, Aspergillus fumigatus growth from airway specimen, elevated serum galactomannan) are included, but the explicit diagnostic statement is omitted.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished invasive aspergillosis from bacterial VAP and CMV reactivation by (a) demonstrating filamentous fungal elements in freshly drained abscesses, (b) isolating A. fumigatus from endotracheal aspiration at a high colony count (10⁵), (c) documenting a positive serum galactomannan (>0.5), and (d) correlating these findings with characteristic chest CT lesions (excavated nodules with ground‑glass halo). Competing bacterial pathogens (P. aeruginosa, K. pneumoniae) were identified in separate VAP episodes but were not recovered from the respiratory specimens obtained at the time of the aspergillosis work‑up. CMV DNA was present in blood and BAL, yet the pulmonary imaging and microbiology were more consistent with fungal invasion.
case_prompt:
The patient, a 55‑year‑old man from Mali, was hospitalized on July 10, 2013 for febrile acute low back pain. His past medical history was unremarkable; he had lived in France for 30 years and returned from Mali in April 2011. He was a smoker, worked as a kitchen porter, and denied alcohol or narcotic use. He reported asthenia, anorexia, 21 kg weight loss (BMI 17), and liquid stools once daily for several weeks.

Initial laboratory tests showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL), CRP 157 mg/L, leukocytes 5.470 ×10³/µL with neutrophilia (83 %) and lymphopenia (15 %), and a CD4 count <200 /mm³; HIV serology was negative.

Abdominal CT on July 12 revealed a right retroperitoneal collection and right colitis. Blood cultures later grew group F Streptococcus, prompting amoxicillin plus gentamicin therapy. Despite antibiotics, the patient progressed to septic shock on August 2 and was transferred to the ICU. Repeat CT showed abscesses of the right kidney, right psoas, and liver, with thickening of the right colon and peritoneal contrast loss. A right hemicolectomy was performed, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin‑tazobactam, fluconazole, amikacin) were started. Cultures from abscesses grew group F Streptococcus and Escherichia coli.

A second septic shock occurred on August 8; CT demonstrated additional abscesses in the liver, retroperitoneum, right kidney, right thigh, and psoas, together with pneumoperitoneum from a sigmoid perforation. After further surgery (right nephrectomy, cholecystectomy) and a regimen of imipenem plus amikacin, histology of the colon showed numerous Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites, and kidney tissue harbored the same organism. Serology for E. histolytica was positive (Latex 1/32; ELISA 5 AU). Anti‑amebic therapy (ornidazole, tiliquinol) was initiated on August 12.

Concurrent renal histology revealed large cells with eosinophilic inclusion bodies; immunohistochemistry identified cytomegalovirus (CMV) antigen. Quantitative PCR detected CMV DNA in blood (20 900 copies/mL) and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (31 800 copies/mL). Ganciclovir therapy began on August 12.

On August 18, the patient experienced another septic shock. Abdominal CT showed new abscesses of the liver, retroperitoneum, right iliopsoas, and right thigh. A third surgical drainage was performed, and antibiotics were broadened to imipenem, vancomycin, and ciprofloxacin. Chest CT revealed excavated nodules surrounded by ground‑glass opacity in both lungs. Macroscopic examination of the newest abdominal abscesses showed fungal filaments, and cultures grew *Aspergillus fumigatus*. Endotracheal aspirate yielded *A. fumigatus* at 10⁵ CFU, and serum galactomannan was elevated to 1.1 (positive > 0.5).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial ventilator‑associated pneumonia (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae) considered because of prior VAP episodes; however, the respiratory specimen at this time grew *Aspergillus fumigatus* and not bacteria, and the lung lesions were nodular rather than consolidative. | "cultures were positive for Aspergillus fumigatus… two VAP episodes documented with Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Klebsiella pneumoniae."
2. Cytomegalovirus pulmonary infection considered given CMV DNA detected in BAL fluid; nevertheless, imaging showed nodules with a halo sign and galactomannan positivity, findings more specific for invasive aspergillosis. | "quantitative PCR detected CMV DNA in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (viral load: 31,800/ml)… chest CT showed excavated nodules surrounded by ground glass opacity… seric galactomanan elevated to 1.1 > 0.5."
3. Invasive amebiasis as cause of abdominal abscesses considered, supported by histology and serology; yet the new abdominal collections contained fungal filaments and yielded *A. fumigatus* on culture, indicating a second pathogen. | "Histological analysis … many Entamoeba histolytic… Macroscopic analysis of the newest abscesses revealed the presence of fungal filaments, and cultures were positive for Aspergillus fumigatus."
4. Other invasive fungal infections (e.g., Candida spp.) were not identified in cultures, and the combination of positive culture, high galactomannan, and characteristic CT findings specifically supports *Aspergillus* infection. | "A. fumigatus grew at 10E5 level in endotracheal aspiration… seric galactomanan elevated to 1.1 > 0.5."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case culminates in a confirmed heterozygous GATA2 missense mutation, diagnosing GATA2 deficiency. This disease is not on the 21 SELECTED list, so it is classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where clinicians “considered a diagnosis of GATA2” but before the PCR sequencing result confirming the mutation. This includes history, physical exam, laboratory and marrow findings, immunophenotyping, and the differential discussion, allowing learners to reason toward a genetic immunodeficiency without the spoiler.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguish GATA2 deficiency from aplastic anemia, low‑grade MDS, HLH, congenital bone‑marrow failure syndromes, common variable immune deficiency, and combined T‑ and B‑cell defects by using cytogenetics, ferritin level, clinical stigmata, immunoglobulin levels, T‑cell counts, infection history, and the specific pattern of monocytopenia, B‑cell lymphocytopenia, and absent dendritic cells.
case_prompt:
A 19‑year‑old white female presented to a hematology clinic for evaluation of aplastic anemia. Her past history included menorrhagia with platelet counts ≈20 × 10³/µL at age 13, a bone‑marrow biopsy at age 14 showing a hypocellular marrow without evidence of leukemia or myelodysplasia, and two units of packed red blood cells transfused at age 16 for anemia (Hb 9.9 g/dL). She reported frequent sinus and urinary tract infections. Family history revealed a maternal grandmother with systemic lupus erythematosus and multiple maternal relatives with chronic anemia and low blood counts.

On examination she appeared well, with mild bruising of the upper extremities, normal cardiopulmonary and abdominal findings, no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, and diffuse superficial aphthous‑like ulcers of the mouth, vagina, and nasopharynx. case_prompt:
A 28‑year‑old South East Asian woman with a history of recurrent abortions presented to the emergency department with a four‑day history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, abdominal distention, nausea, and recurrent vomiting. She denied cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, joint pain, skin rash, oral ulcers, and palpitations. There was no prior similar episode, no alcohol use, and no home medications.

On admission she was conscious, oriented, and in mild distress. Vital signs: respiratory rate 25/min, temperature 39 °C. Physical examination revealed mild epigastric tenderness, abdominal distention, a few bibasilar crackles, and normal heart sounds.

Laboratory studies: hemoglobin 13 g/dL, platelets 71 × 10³/µL, white blood cell count 14 × 10³/µL, lipase >3300 U/L, amylase 960 U/L, aPTT 67.8 s, D‑dimer 2.96 mg/L FEU, ALT 14 U/L, AST 16 U/L, ALP 48 U/L, total bilirubin 14 µmol/L, lactate 0.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 0.8 ng/mL, LDH 794 U/L, CRP 323 mg/L.

Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen showed ill‑defined hypodensities in the pancreatic tail with irregular outlines and peripancreatic fluid. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a normal ejection fraction of 50 % without structural abnormalities.

The patient was initially managed for acute pancreatitis with intravenous fluids and analgesics. Over the next few days she deteriorated, developing persistent abdominal pain, recurrent fever spikes, worsening dyspnea, and hypoxemia. Chest X‑ray revealed increased left lower‑zone opacity, retro‑cardiac density suggestive of collapse, and a left‑sided pleural effusion. Repeat echocardiography showed global hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 20‑25 % and no vegetations.

Laboratory trends now showed rising liver enzymes (ALT 196 U/L, AST 194 U/L), ALP 148 U/L, total bilirubin 64.5 µmol/L (direct 40 µmol/L). The patient required intensive‑care admission.

Septic workup with broad‑range cultures was negative. A viral hepatitis panel was positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) PCR with 5,863 copies; she received two weeks of ganciclovir with little clinical improvement despite clearance of CMV viremia. Abdominal imaging demonstrated persistent peripancreatic inflammation, heterogeneous enhancement of the right posterior hepatic segments, and segmental portal vein thrombosis.

Given the prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia, and history of recurrent abortions, an autoimmune workup was performed to evaluate catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. Results were: ANA positive (1:160, speckled), anti‑dsDNA equivocal (11), C3 93 mg/dL, C4 16 mg/dL, ANCA negative, anticardiolipin IgM negative, anticardiolipin IgG positive (20 mg/dL), anti‑β2‑glycoprotein I IgM positive (30 mg/dL).

Her abdominal symptoms also showed minimal resolution in contrast to the biochemical improvement in acute pancreatitis."

case_prompt:
A 63‑year‑old woman with end‑stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy (kidney transplant in 1995) presented with six‑month history of generalized malaise, exertional dyspnea, and cough. Her comorbidities included type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic allograft dysfunction. Immunosuppression consisted of cyclosporine 100 mg q12 h, azathioprine 50 mg daily, and prednisone 5 mg daily. On arrival she was hypotensive (BP 75/48 mmHg) and febrile (100.6 °F). Norepinephrine and broad‑spectrum antibiotics were started, although no obvious infection source was identified. Laboratory studies showed anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated LDH and CRP. Morning cortisol was low (0.6 µg/dL), prompting stress‑dose hydrocortisone. Her hypotension and fever improved within 24 h and she was discharged.

Over the next two months she was readmitted four times for fever, shock, and fatigue, each time responding rapidly to stress‑dose steroids and vasopressors, often without a clear diagnosis. CMV viremia had previously been detected, but subsequent episodes occurred despite undetectable CMV load on valganciclovir therapy.

On a fifth admission she again had hypotension and fever. Review of systems was otherwise negative, and physical examination was unremarkable. Labs revealed WBC 7,200/mm³, hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, platelets 83 × 10³/mm³, LDH 410 IU/L, CRP 153 mg/L, mildly elevated AST/ALT (50/41 IU/L), triglycerides 547 mg/dL, and ferritin 3 311 ng/mL. CMV PCR was negative. Vasopressor support and stress‑dose hydrocortisone were given, with prompt hemodynamic improvement. Chest/abdomen/pelvis CT showed patchy ground‑glass opacities at both lung apices. Broncho‑alveolar lavage yielded no pathogens, including Pneumocystis jirovecii. Additional testing was performed to exclude rheumatologic disease, macrophage activation syndrome, malignancy, and autoinflammatory syndromes. Complement levels were normal; antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor were negative. Serum protein electrophoresis showed normal immunoglobulins and no monoclonal spike. EBV PCR was negative.

Patient 1 was identified on newborn screening because of abnormally low T‑cell receptor excision circles (TRECs). There was no maternal engraftment and HIV testing was negative. Physical examination at presentation was normal. Prophylaxis with IVIG, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, and fluconazole was started at 1 week of age. Laboratory evaluation confirmed a T‑B‑NK⁺ severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) with profound T‑ and B‑cell lymphopenia and a markedly reduced response to phytohemagglutinin (≈2 % of normal). The patient also had neutropenia (absolute neutrophil count 200 cells/µL). A comprehensive SCID genetic panel identified a heterozygous pathogenic RMRP variant but no second allele and no clinical features of cartilage‑hair hypoplasia. By 2 months of age he developed diarrhea and was found to be CMV PCR‑positive in blood; valganciclovir therapy was initiated. Because an HLA‑matched unrelated donor or cord blood unit was unavailable, he received an emergent maternal haploidentical CD3/CD19‑depleted hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) two weeks later, after reduced‑intensity conditioning with thymoglobulin and busulfan. He became CMV PCR‑negative two weeks post‑transplant. At discharge he remained on fluconazole, pentamidine, IVIG, and treatment‑dose foscarnet. At 3 months post‑transplant he developed autoimmune hemolytic anemia, treated with methylprednisone. He was hospitalized at 5 and 7 months for Enterobacter septicemia related to his central line. Progressive neutropenia persisted, requiring thrice‑weekly G‑CSF to keep the absolute neutrophil count above 500 cells/µL. At 16 months post‑HCT, T‑cell engraftment was 83 % with normal CD3 counts, but TRECs remained low, myeloid engraftment was absent, B‑cell numbers were poor, IgA and IgM were low, and immunoglobulin replacement continued. Bone‑marrow biopsy showed normocellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis; CMV PCR remained negative.  

At 3 years and 2.5 months of age, a second HCT using TCR α/β‑depleted peripheral blood stem cells from the same donor was performed because of ongoing immune reconstitution defects. Myeloablative conditioning consisted of fludarabine, melphalan, thiotepa, and thymoglobulin. Neutrophil recovery (>1,000 cells/µL) occurred by day 10, and 100 % donor engraftment was documented at 3 months. The patient experienced CMV reactivation resistant to foscarnet, which responded to CMV‑specific cytotoxic T‑cells. At 3 months post‑second transplant he developed polyserositis of unclear etiology manifested as pericardial and pleural effusions, which progressed to acute respiratory distress syndrome and pulmonary hemorrhage, culminating in death.

3. HIV infection was ruled out, eliminating an acquired cause of lymphopenia. | "HIV testing was negative."
4. Cartilage‑Hair Hypoplasia was considered due to an RMRP variant but excluded because only a heterozygous carrier state was found and no clinical features were present. | "A ... panel demonstrated him to be a carrier of a heterozygous pathogenic variant in RMRP, with neither an identified second variant nor any features of Cartilage‑Hair Hypoplasia."

6. case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old woman, six years post renal transplantation, presented with a 36‑hour history of fever, hypotension, and asthenia accompanied by a 7‑kg weight loss over the preceding three months. Physical examination showed oral white plaques and a maculopapular rash on the back. Laboratory studies revealed anemia (Hb 8.4 g/dL, Ht 23 %), leukopenia (2.3 × 10⁹/L), elevated C‑reactive protein (10.8 mg/dL) and ferritin (13 253 ng/mL), and acute graft dysfunction (serum creatinine rising from a baseline of 3.0 mg/dL to >4.0 mg/dL). Liver enzymes were within normal limits. Immunosuppression consisted of prednisone 5 mg/day and azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day. 

On admission, blood cultures were obtained for fungi and mycobacteria. PCR assays for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV), a latex agglutination test for cryptococcus, and serologies for Histoplasma capsulatum and Trypanosoma cruzi were ordered. Empiric therapy with vancomycin, meropenem, and ganciclovir was started to cover possible bacterial or viral opportunistic infection. CMV antigenemia was negative, but PCR detected 546 copies of CMV DNA. 

A skin‑lesion biopsy and fungal/mycobacterial cultures were performed. Thoraco‑abdominal CT scan and transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities. Bone‑marrow aspiration demonstrated erythroid hyperplasia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed ulcerative esophagitis with intranuclear inclusions and focal candidal plaques; fluconazole was added to the regimen. 

The patient’s condition deteriorated, developing melena, mucocutaneous bleeding, hemodynamic instability, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Empiric liposomal amphotericin B was initiated to cover histoplasmosis, and a four‑drug antitubercular regimen was started. She required mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, and subsequently developed amphotericin‑related hepatotoxicity, culminating in death seven days after initiating antifungal therapy.

Histoplasmosis suspected based on oral candidiasis, cutaneous rash, ulcerative esophagitis with intranuclear inclusions, marked weight loss, anemia, leukopenia, and markedly elevated ferritin; empirical liposomal amphotericin B was added to cover this infection | "We empirically started liposomal amphotericin B to cover histoplasmosis..."

case_prompt:
An 8‑year‑old boy from Limpopo, South Africa, with a history of premature birth, chronic undernutrition (weight‑for‑age z score = ‑2, BMI = 13), and a 2‑year history of abdominal distension, diarrhoea, night sweats and failure to thrive was referred to paediatric gastroenterology in October 2016. He had recent travel to Kruger National Park and India six months earlier. Vaccination history was reported as up‑to‑date, but not verified.

On admission he was acutely ill, severely wasted (17 kg), febrile (39 °C), pale, tachycardic and had mild lower‑limb oedema. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly without peripheral lymphadenopathy; the abdomen was markedly distended with recurrent diarrhoea and vomiting and food intolerance.

Abdominal CT and ultrasound showed massively enlarged intra‑abdominal lymph nodes with a “moth‑eaten” spleen and prominent collateral vessels suggesting portal hypertension.

Laboratory studies showed HIV infection with CD4 = 59 cells/µL (7%) and HIV viral load = 453 780 copies/mL. Mildly elevated transaminases, moderate proteinuria, fecal alpha‑1 antitrypsin consistent with protein‑losing enteropathy, and microcytic hypochromic anaemia with reticuloendothelial iron blockade were noted.

The initial differential diagnosis emphasized tuberculosis or lymphoma. Over 7 months, endoscopic and surgical biopsies of duodenal and lymph‑node tissue were obtained. Histology was interpreted as consistent with a non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection.

Acid‑fast bacilli were identified on lymph‑node tissue (12 Oct 2016) and on a repeat biopsy (8 Mar 2017). Stool microscopy (26 Mar 2017) also revealed acid‑fast organisms with a coccoid appearance. PCR assays for Mycobacterium avium complex were negative, as were multiple PCR platforms for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (Nanogen, BD MAX, Xpert MTB/RIF). Urinary lipoarabinomannan testing (22 Mar 2017) was positive.

A CMV viraemia of 3 974 copies/mL and a colon biopsy PCR positive for CMV were recorded in March 2017, as was an Epstein‑Barr virus load of 9 318 copies/mL.

1. Tuberculosis considered due to fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and intra‑abdominal lymphadenopathy; excluded because multiple PCR assays for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex were negative and cultures yielded no growth. | "Numerous PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex were negative... With a failing pancreas graft, linagliptin was initiated and pancreatectomy was considered, but the absence of overt bleeding led the team to pursue a comprehensive haematological work‑up.

Lumbar puncture demonstrated a CSF white‑blood‑cell count of 103 cells/mm³ (55 % lymphocytes, 7 % neutrophils, 8 % monocytes), glucose 56 mg/dL, protein 180 mg/dL, opening pressure 15 cm H₂O. Empiric therapy with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, ampicillin, and acyclovir was started. CSF studies were negative for cryptococcal antigen, Lyme IgM, Toxoplasma IgG, varicella, VDRL, and CMV; HSV PCR was pending. Gram stain, bacterial culture, and fungal culture showed no growth by hospital day 3. The patient improved rapidly and was discharged on acyclovir with a presumptive diagnosis of viral meningitis.

One day after discharge he returned with new right‑sided weakness and dysarthria. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with parenchymal enhancement in the left frontal lobe. Viral meningitis was the provisional diagnosis after the first admission because the patient “rapidly improved and was discharged with suspected viral meningitis on acyclovir,” yet the subsequent relapse with focal neurologic deficits and MRI enhancement is atypical for uncomplicated viral disease.

5. Tuberculous meningitis and neurosyphilis were excluded early: serologic VDRL and CSF VDRL were negative (“VDRL…negative”), and there was no mention of acid‑fast bacilli or elevated CSF opening pressure typical of TB meningitis.

A 68‑year‑old man with a past history of ischemic stroke (2015) and hypertension presented to the emergency department with a 3‑month history of asthenia, anorexia, night sweats (occasionally with perceived fever), and a 2‑week history of intermittent fever. Three days before admission he noted a pruritic maculopapular rash on the trunk and back. He denied immunosuppression or relevant epidemiologic exposures.

Current medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril, and oral terbinafine 250 mg, which had been stopped after one week because of a “sickness sensation.”

On examination he was febrile (38.9 °C), tachycardic, and had hard, painless, immobile lymphadenopathy in the supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions, with nodes up to 3–4 cm. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, absolute eosinophilia (up to 3.52 × 10⁹/L), elevated cholestatic enzymes (AST 142 U/L, ALT 161 U/L, ALP 166 U/L), total bilirubin 1.92 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 798 IU/L, mild ionized hypercalcemia (1.51 mmol/L), and C‑reactive protein >100 mg/L. Peripheral smear, protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, free light chains, and serum/urine immunofixation were normal; proteinuria was absent. Serial blood cultures remained negative.

During admission he continued to experience daily fever spikes despite antipyretics and developed purulent tonsillitis with progressive odynophagia and solid dysphagia. Empiric clindamycin was started, later supplemented with ceftriaxone due to poor clinical response. The rash spread centrifugally to the limbs, became symmetric and coalescent without vesicles or blisters, and Nikolsky sign was negative; facial swelling was noted without mucosal involvement. Pruritus was controlled with antihistamines.

Virologic testing revealed high HHV‑6 DNA (230,000 copies/mL) and CMV DNA (5,010 IU/mL); EBV DNA was low (≈500 copies/mL) and parvovirus DNA <150 copies/mL. HIV, HBV, HCV, and VZV serologies were negative.

Given the temporal association with terbinafine, a presumptive diagnosis of DRESS syndrome was made and topical betamethasone was initiated, leading to resolution of the skin findings over 14 days. Oral steroids were avoided to not mask a possible lymphoproliferative process. Persistent B symptoms and poor response to antibiotics raised suspicion for a lymphoproliferative neoplasm involving the Waldeyer ring. Tonsillar scrapings showed nonspecific necrotizing inflammation; EBV PCR from the tonsil was positive; anti‑streptolysin O titer was negative. The antimicrobial course was completed.

To obtain a definitive diagnosis, an excisional biopsy of an inguinal lymph node was performed.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on infective endocarditis caused by MRSA leading to pulmonary artery perforation and haemopericardium. Infective endocarditis is not in the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so the final diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.

case_prompt:
An 18‑year‑old male presented with a 12‑day history of sudden‑onset, high‑grade, continuous fever with rigors. He had been managed initially as a presumed dengue case based on serology (positive IgM, negative IgG). Eight days after illness onset he developed left‑sided chest pain that worsened when lying flat and improved on leaning forward. He denied dysuria, diarrhoea, productive cough, or headache. Past medical history was notable for a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). He reported contact with his grandfather, who had active tuberculosis.

On admission his blood pressure was 140/80 mm Hg, pulse 140 bpm, temperature 101 °F, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. General examination showed pallor; there were no puncture marks, jugular venous distension, or engorged neck veins. Cardiac examination revealed a machinery murmur at the left second intercostal space; no pericardial rub was heard. Lung auscultation was normal except for decreased air entry at the left base. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia with concave ST‑segment elevation and PR depression in leads I, II, aVL, V2, with reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation in aVR. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, leukocytosis 17 × 10⁹/L, and ESR 60 mm/h. Blood cultures grew methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Dengue IgM remained positive; tuberculosis immunochromatographic test was negative. Chest radiograph showed an increased cardiothoracic ratio, prominent left pulmonary artery markings, and bilateral irregular opacities. Two‑dimensional echocardiography revealed circumferential pericardial effusion and a small PDA with normal left ventricular function.

Twelve hours after admission the patient developed acute shortness of breath, worsening chest pain, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, and heart rate 150 bpm, raising concern for impending cardiac tamponade. A pericardial window and PDA ligation were planned. Infective endocarditis associated with the PDA was considered because of one major criterion (positive blood culture) and three minor criteria (fever >38 °C, predisposing cardiac lesion, and septic pulmonary emboli on CT). The CT chest demonstrated infiltrates in the lung fields consistent with septic emboli.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue fever considered initially due to positive IgM serology but excluded because bacteremia with MRSA and presence of murmur, PDA, and septic emboli are atypical for dengue; "The patient was initially managed as a presumed case of dengue fever based on serology: positive Ig M antibody and negative Ig G antibody."
2. Tuberculosis considered given household exposure, but excluded by negative tuberculosis ICT and lack of classic TB pericarditis features; "the tuberculosis ICT was negative."
3. Isolated viral or idiopathic pericardial effusion considered but ruled out by identification of a bacterial pathogen in blood cultures and vascular phenomena; "Blood cultures showed growth of methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus."
4. Infective endocarditis favored as the unifying diagnosis because it fulfills Duke’s criteria (one major: positive blood culture; three minor: fever, predisposing cardiac lesion, septic emboli) and explains the pericardial effusion and pulmonary findings; "Infective endocarditis in association with PDA was considered a possibility due to the presence of one major criterion and three minor criteria: the Duke's criteria."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case describes subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis following dengue infection. No disease from the 21 SELECTED list is present, so the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation up to the thyroid scintigraphy result (absence of radionuclide uptake) and the fine‑needle aspiration result, but stop before any statement about the definitive diagnosis or treatment outcome. This provides enough clinical, laboratory, and imaging data for the learner to infer subacute thyroiditis without revealing the diagnosis directly.
3. Key analytic distinctions: The authors distinguished thyroiditis from malignant nodule (ultrasound‑guided FNA Bethesda II) and from Graves disease (negative thyroid antibodies and absent radionuclide uptake on scintigraphy). The pattern of low TSH, elevated free T4/T3, painful thyroid enlargement, and transient thyrotoxic phase supported subacute thyroiditis.
case_prompt: A 38‑year‑old woman from Sullana, Piura, Peru, previously healthy, was diagnosed with dengue (positive IgM ELISA) and received outpatient symptomatic care. Four weeks later she developed intense pain in the anterior cervical region radiating to the mandible and auricular area, along with swelling of that region, general malaise, odynophagia, dysphagia, palpitations, and limb tremor. Cervical ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous thyroid gland and, in the left lobe, a solid, hypoechogenic nodule with irregular margins measuring 27 × 15 mm, classified as ACR‑TIRADS 4. Multiple enlarged, rounded cervical lymph nodes with well‑defined contours and increased vascular flow were also noted. The patient experienced marked cervical pain when the transducer contacted the neck. On admission she had palpitations and resting tremor suggestive of thyrotoxicosis. Laboratory tests showed TSH 0.043 IUI/mL, elevated free T4 and free T3, negative anti‑thyroperoxidase and anti‑thyroglobulin antibodies, and elevated serum thyroglobulin. Thyroid scintigraphy with Technetium‑99m demonstrated absence of radionuclide uptake. Because of the suspicious ultrasound nodule, an ultrasound‑guided fine‑needle aspiration was performed, yielding a Bethesda II (benign) result.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Painful thyroid enlargement with transient thyrotoxic symptoms suggests subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis | "intense pain in the anterior cervical region ... palpitations and tremor at rest, compatible with signs of thyrotoxicosis."
2. Low TSH with elevated free T4/T3, negative thyroid autoantibodies, and elevated thyroglobulin point toward inflammatory destruction rather than autoimmune hyperthyroidism | "TSH was found at 0.043 ... elevated free thyroxine (T4L) and free triiodothyronine (T3L), negative antithyroperoxidase antibodies (ATPO) and antithyroglobulin antibodies (ATG), and elevated thyroglobulin levels."
3. Absence of radionuclide uptake on technetium‑99m scan supports thyroiditis and excludes Graves disease, which shows increased uptake | "Thyroid scintigraphy with Technetium-99m showed absence of radionuclide uptake, compatible with thyroiditis."
4. Ultrasound‑guided fine‑needle aspiration yielding Bethesda II rules out malignancy despite a TIRADS 4 nodule | "the result was Bethesda II."
5. The presence of cervical lymphadenopathy could suggest malignancy or infection, but its benign sonographic features (well‑defined, homogeneous, hyperechogenic hilum) and resolution with steroids favor inflammatory thyroiditis | "multiple adenopathies ... enlarged, rounded, with well‑defined contours, homogeneous structure, hyperechogenic lymph node hilum and increased vascular flow."
6. Dengue infection preceded the thyroid event, providing a plausible viral trigger for subacute thyroiditis | "previously healthy ... was diagnosed with dengue without alarm signs ... Four weeks later, she presented intense pain ..."

Subdural hematoma is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; dengue is, but it is presented only as a prior confirmed infection (IgM‑positive) without requiring diagnostic work‑up here. Therefore the target diagnosis is the OUT_OF_SCOPE condition “subdural hematoma”.
2. case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department after a sudden loss of consciousness lasting one hour. The day before, he had experienced a severe headache with nausea and more than five episodes of vomiting. His family denied seizures, limb weakness, facial droop, or prior head trauma. His past medical history was significant for hypertension (untreated) and hospitalization five days earlier for dengue hemorrhagic fever, during which laboratory testing showed thrombocytopenia (30,000/µL) and a positive IgM dengue antibody; he was discharged on day 4.

On arrival, he was unresponsive, febrile (38.6 °C), and hypertensive (160/90 mm Hg). Pulse was 102/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO₂ 97 % on room air. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3/15, no meningeal irritation, and anisocoric pupils (right 6 mm, left 2 mm) with absent light reflexes. Laboratory tests showed normal glucose (136 mg/dL), persistent thrombocytopenia (74 × 10³/µL), hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, normal leukocyte count, coagulation profile, and renal function.

A chest X‑ray demonstrated mild cardiomegaly. Non‑contrast CT of the head revealed a wide, hyperdense lesion in the right frontotemporoparietal region extending to the falx cerebri, with a hypodense transition suggestive of a subacute subdural hematoma. Midline shift, a narrowed left ventricle, and surrounding cerebral edema were also noted.

1. Subdural hematoma suggested by CT morphology – “CT scan showed a wide, hyperdense lesion… with a hypodense transition suggestive of a subacute SDH” |
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage considered less likely because the lesion is extra‑axial and conforms to the falx, not typical of parenchymal bleed – “hyperdense lesion… extending to the falc cerebri” |
3. Meningitis/encephalitis excluded by lack of meningeal signs – “without signs of meningeal irritation” |
4. Metabolic encephalopathy deemed unlikely given focal mass effect and anisocoric pupils – “midline shift… cerebral edema… anisocoric pupils with a negative light reflex” |
5. Infectious process (bacterial meningitis) considered, prompting empiric ceftriaxone, but imaging did not support meningeal enhancement – “antibiotics, ceftriaxone injection… were also given” |

case_prompt: A 28‑year‑old woman was hospitalized for acute‑onset high fever, myalgia, arthralgia and ocular pain. case_prompt:
A 19‑year‑old male with no known comorbidities presented to an outside hospital after two weeks of high‑grade fever and a productive cough with scant sputum. Physical examination revealed decreased air entry on the right side with a stony‑dull percussion note. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel, but an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/hour. Chest radiography demonstrated blunting of the right costo‑phrenic angle consistent with a right‑sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocytic‑predominant pleural fluid, leading to a clinical diagnosis of tuberculous pleuritis and initiation of four‑drug antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).

The regimen required several modifications because of adverse drug reactions: pyrazinamide caused hyperuricemia, ofloxacin produced severe gastrointestinal symptoms, streptomycin induced vertiginous otologic toxicity, and ethambutol caused bilateral optic neuritis confirmed by visual evoked potentials. The rash consisted of papules and vesicles filled with clear fluid, with subsequent skin peeling over the entire body and oral mucosa. Conjunctival membranes were involved, with eyelid edema and mucopurulent discharge.

On examination the child appeared sick, was febrile and irritable, but hemodynamically stable. He had a plethoric complexion, generalized vesiculobullous rash with desquamation, hepatosplenomegaly, and otherwise normal findings on other system examinations.

- Malarial antigen test (negative)
- Serology for dengue, chikungunya, leptospirosis, and rickettsia (negative)
- Direct Coombs test and antinuclear antibody (non‑contributory)

On admission his vitals were pulse 140 bpm, blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, capillary refill <2 s; hematocrit had risen 16.7 % from his baseline (42 % on admission, baseline 36 %). Within 24 h he developed vomiting and abdominal pain, without bleeding. Examination revealed generalized flushing, right hypochondrial tenderness, a 3‑cm hepatomegaly, and no signs of plasma leakage. Point‑of‑care ultrasound showed a mild pleural effusion and a thickened gall‑bladder wall.

Investigations during hospitalization showed leucopenia (2.2 × 10³/µL), thrombocytopenia (68 × 10³/µL), and elevated transaminases (ALT 88 U/L, AST 124 U/L). C‑reactive protein and renal function were normal. He was managed as dengue hemorrhagic fever in a high‑dependency unit. Platelet count fell to a nadir of 6 × 10³/µL on day 7, but he had no bleeding manifestations. Dengue IgM and IgG were positive on day 7. He recovered, with platelet count rising to 52 × 10³/µL by day 11; discharge labs showed WBC 7.5 × 10³/µL and platelets 52 × 10³/µL. Follow‑up at two weeks showed platelets 47 × 10³/µL; at one month, platelets 100 × 10³/µL.

One year later he returned with a one‑week history of multiple purpura. Review of home‑performed counts documented persistent thrombocytopenia ranging from 30‑45 × 10³/µL. Serologies for Mycoplasma, influenza, cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and Epstein‑Barr virus were negative. Baseline immunoglobulins and complement levels were normal, and there was no recent MMR vaccination or use of platelet‑lowering drugs. Peripheral blood film showed normal cell morphology with isolated thrombocytopenia. Bone‑marrow examination revealed megakaryocytes with otherwise normal trilineage hematopoiesis.

Computed tomography confirmed a 15‑cm splenic cyst with parietal calcifications compressing the stomach, described as “most likely of hydatid origin.” MRI showed a unilocular cyst that was hypo‑intense on T1 and hyper‑intense on T2. Differential diagnosis included splenic abscess, hydatid cyst, epithelial cyst, and post‑traumatic hemorrhage in a pre‑existing epithelial cyst. Serologic testing for HBV, HCV, CMV, HIV, toxoplasmosis, Entamoeba histolytica, Leishmania spp., and EBV IgM were negative; EBV IgG was positive for prior exposure. Immunodiffusion for *Echinococcus multilocularis* and indirect hemagglutination and ELISA for *E. granulosus* were also negative. An elevated IgE level of 317 kU/L led clinicians to treat the lesion as a hydatid cyst with albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 28 days and administration of the anti‑pneumococcal vaccine. Because of severe continuous pain, large cyst size, risk of rupture, and the patient’s desire to resume horse riding, she underwent laparotomy for cyst un‑roofing and partial splenectomy. Intra‑operatively, the abdomen was protected with 3 % NaCl pads, 2 L of dark‑green fluid was aspirated from the cyst, hypertonic saline was injected and later removed, and the cyst wall was partially resected. The postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged on postoperative day 5.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies a CNS infection with Cryptococcus (cryptococcosis), which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Present the case up to the point where initial pathology suggested an Echinococcus/hydatid cyst and extensive serologic testing was negative, but before the second‑opinion pathology and the positive Cryptococcus antigen result are disclosed. This provides enough clinical, imaging, and laboratory data for the learner to consider and work toward cryptococcosis without revealing it.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated diagnoses by (a) neuro‑imaging characteristics (enhancing masses vs. metastasis/abscess), (b) histopathology with special stains (PAS, GMS, mucicarmine) that can highlight both parasitic cyst walls and fungal organisms, (c) negative acid‑fast bacilli stain to exclude TB, (d) a broad serologic panel that was uniformly negative (including Echinococcus), and (e) CSF cultures and antigen assays that were initially negative for Cryptococcus, prompting a second pathological review that identified cryptococcal organisms and a subsequently positive antigen test.
case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old man presented after a witnessed new‑onset seizure. He described sudden numbness of his left third through fifth digits, followed by shaking of his left hand and a “locking” sensation; he then awoke on the floor confused about his surroundings. He denied presyncope, incontinence, tongue‑biting, or myalgias. Past medical and surgical history were unremarkable; he uses marijuana and has traveled to Mexico (5 years ago) and Puerto Rico (7 years ago). 

Non‑contrast head CT showed hypodense areas in the right frontoparietal and left parieto‑occipital lobes. MRI with and without contrast demonstrated enhancing masses suspicious for metastasis versus abscesses associated with vasogenic edema, without midline shift. 

On hospital day 6, he underwent left parietal craniectomy with resection of the left parieto‑occipital lesion. Pathology revealed fragments of non‑epithelialized fibrous cyst wall containing neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, focal necrosis, and numerous small cystic structures. Special stains were positive for periodic acid‑Schiff, Gomori’s methenamine silver, and mucicarmine, and negative for acid‑fast bacilli. The findings were interpreted as consistent with the walls of an Echinococcus/hydatid cyst. 

Comprehensive laboratory testing—including HIV, rapid plasma reagin, toxoplasma IgG/IgM, Lyme serology, cytomegalovirus, tuberculosis, cysticercosis, and Echinococcus serology—was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid culture yielded no growth, and multiple CSF Cryptococcus antigen assays were negative.
